name: Afghanistan
cuisine_summary: Afghan cuisine is one of Central Asia's most refined — long-grain rice perfumed with saffron, cardamom, and dried fruit; lamb marinated in yogurt and grilled over charcoal; and flatbreads baked directly on clay oven walls. Persian delicacy meets Silk Road spice. Kabuli pulao, the national dish, is a study in patience: slow-cooked rice layered with caramelized carrots, raisins, and tender lamb. It is food built for hospitality and ceremony.
dish1_desc: The national dish. Basmati rice cooked with lamb, topped with caramelized carrots and raisins. Fragrant, rich, and made for a crowd.
dish2_desc: Steamed dumplings filled with spiced ground beef and onion, draped in yogurt and a garlicky tomato sauce.
dish3_desc: Flatbread stuffed with potato, leek, or spinach and pan-fried until crispy. The everyday street food and tea-time snack.

name: Albania
cuisine_summary: Albanian cuisine is where the Mediterranean and the Balkans quietly negotiate — olive-oil-drenched vegetables, slow-grilled meats, and thick salted yogurt that appears at nearly every meal. Tavë kosi, the national dish, is a baked lamb and rice custard set in tangy yogurt and eggs — rich, custardy, deeply satisfying. Byrek (flaky filo filled with spinach, white cheese, or spiced meat) turns up at every bakery. The cooking is unpretentious and ingredient-honest, with centuries of Ottoman and Byzantine history underneath.
dish1_desc: Baked lamb and rice set in a tangy yogurt-egg custard. Albania's national dish — rich, custardy, and deeply satisfying.
dish2_desc: Flaky filo pastry filled with spinach and white cheese, or spiced meat. Found in every bakery, eaten at any hour.
dish3_desc: Roasted peppers and tomatoes baked with cottage cheese and olive oil. A staple of Tirana — simple, warming, vegetarian.

name: Algeria
cuisine_summary: Algerian cuisine draws on Berber, Arab, Ottoman, and French influences — slow-cooked couscous, spiced lamb stews, and merguez sausages sizzling over charcoal at street-side grills.
dish1_desc: Steamed semolina piled with lamb or chicken and seven vegetables in a spiced broth. The Friday family meal, non-negotiable.
dish2_desc: Spiced lamb soup with cracked freekeh wheat, tomatoes, chickpeas, and fresh coriander. The Ramadan table's anchor dish.
dish3_desc: Spicy lamb-and-beef sausages grilled over charcoal, eaten stuffed in a baguette or alongside flatbread.

name: Andorra
cuisine_summary: Andorran cuisine is Pyrenean mountain food — hearty enough to fuel a day of altitude and physical labor. It shares its soul with Catalan cooking: trinxat (mashed cabbage and potato fried with bacon into a golden cake), escudella (a slow winter stew of pork, sausage, and root vegetables), and cured mountain meats aged in cold air. French and Spanish influences converge naturally in this tiny nation — the wine is Catalan, the cheese is French, and the cooking is entirely its own.
dish1_desc: Thick winter stew of pork, sausage, pasta, and root vegetables. The Andorran Sunday lunch when the mountains are cold.
dish2_desc: Mashed cabbage and potato formed into a cake and fried with bacon. Simple, warming, and pure Pyrenean comfort.
dish3_desc: Snails cooked with garlic, parsley, and olive oil. A mountain delicacy shared with neighboring Catalonia.

name: Angola
cuisine_summary: Angolan food is built on cassava, palm oil, and beans — indigenous West African tradition layered with a Portuguese colonial legacy. Fish from the Atlantic coast and piri piri heat run through everything.
dish1_desc: Chicken stewed in red palm oil with garlic, okra, and piri piri chiles. Angola's national dish — rich, orange, deeply savory.
dish2_desc: Smooth cassava porridge, the everyday staple. Neutral, filling, and the required companion to every stew and fish dish.
dish3_desc: Dried fish stewed with palm oil, okra, sweet potato leaves, and onion. An ancient dish, still on every table.

name: Antigua and Barbuda
cuisine_summary: Antiguan food is Caribbean sunshine — salted fish, spiced pepperpot stew, and cornmeal dumplings. The official national dish is fungee and pepperpot, and rum is present at every occasion.
dish1_desc: The national dish. Okra-studded cornmeal dumpling paired with a thick, spiced stew of greens and salted meat.
dish2_desc: Sweet dumplings of grated sweet potato and coconut, steamed in banana leaves. Always served alongside saltfish.
dish3_desc: Stewed conch in a savory broth with lime and hot peppers. A seaside staple, eaten as soup or a light lunch.

name: Argentina
cuisine_summary: Argentine cuisine is the art of the asado — open-fire grilling elevated to a social ritual. Entire cuts of beef, pork ribs, and blood sausage go over slow wood-burning coals, dressed only in chimichurri. Away from the grill: empanadas baked in stone ovens, milanesa (breaded and fried cutlets) eaten at any hour, and locro (a corn-and-bean stew) in the winter. The Mendoza wine valleys produce Malbec that belongs on any world list. Argentina feeds itself with an Italian immigrant's love of food and a gaucho's pride in the flame.
dish1_desc: Hand pies stuffed with seasoned beef, chicken, or cheese. Baked, not fried — the everyday Argentine snack.
dish2_desc: Mixed grill of beef cuts, sausages, and offal. The Sunday family ritual.
dish3_desc: Bright herbaceous sauce of parsley, garlic, vinegar, and oil — the steak's required companion.

name: Armenia
cuisine_summary: Armenian cuisine is ancient and deeply flavored — lamb grilled over vine cuttings, grape leaves simmered in lemon broth, and lavash flatbread baked directly on the wall of a clay oven.
dish1_desc: Armenian-style barbecue: pork, lamb, or chicken marinated and grilled over charcoal. The national pastime and the center of any celebration.
dish2_desc: Grape leaves stuffed with spiced lamb and rice, simmered slowly in a lemon broth until tender. Patient, perfect.
dish3_desc: Tiny oven-baked dumplings filled with spiced minced meat, served with yogurt, sumac, and browned butter. Worth every fold.

name: Australia
cuisine_summary: Australian food is a multicultural barbecue — Indigenous bush ingredients, British working-class staples, and a modern dining scene shaped by waves of Asian and Mediterranean immigration. Casualness is the point.
dish1_desc: Minced beef in gravy inside a short-crust pastry shell. The football ground staple — eaten with a squirt of tomato sauce.
dish2_desc: Native river fish, grilled or pan-fried. Clean, firm white flesh that appears on both beachside fish-and-chip counters and fine-dining menus.
dish3_desc: Sponge cake squares dipped in chocolate icing and rolled in desiccated coconut. The quintessential Australian morning-tea cake.

name: Austria
cuisine_summary: Austrian cuisine is Vienna's coffee-house culture and Alpine heartiness in equal measure — breaded veal cutlets, dumplings in clear broth, and glass cases of pastries you can stare at for ten minutes before choosing.
dish1_desc: Veal pounded thin, breaded, and pan-fried in butter until golden and airy. Served with lemon and a spoonful of lingonberry.
dish2_desc: Boiled beef in broth with root vegetables, served sliced with apple-horseradish sauce. The Viennese Sunday lunch of emperors and families alike.
dish3_desc: Gossamer pastry wrapped around spiced apple and raisins, baked until flaky. Best served warm with vanilla sauce.

name: Azerbaijan
cuisine_summary: Azerbaijani cuisine sits at the Silk Road crossroads — saffron-yellow rice with lamb and dried fruit, pomegranate-soured stews, and lavash stuffed with handfuls of fresh herbs.
dish1_desc: Saffron-scented rice layered with lamb, chestnuts, and dried apricots, sealed and slow-cooked. The centerpiece of every celebration.
dish2_desc: Grape leaves, quince, or cabbage stuffed with spiced lamb and rice, simmered in a tart pomegranate broth.
dish3_desc: Tiny lamb dumplings served in a sour broth with dried mint and a splash of vinegar. Fiddly to fold, impossible to stop eating.

name: Bahamas
cuisine_summary: Bahamian food is the sea on a plate — conch in every form (cracked, stewed, in salad), freshly caught fish, and johnnycakes. Simple, sun-drenched, and entirely tied to the ocean.
dish1_desc: Conch pounded thin, battered, and deep-fried until golden. Served with peas and rice or coleslaw — the island's essential plate.
dish2_desc: Raw conch diced with tomato, onion, bell pepper, and lime juice. The Bahamian ceviche, made to order at roadside shacks.
dish3_desc: Pigeon peas cooked with rice, tomato, and thyme. The island's foundational side dish, eaten alongside almost everything.

name: Bahrain
cuisine_summary: Bahraini food is spiced Gulf cooking with a pearl-diving heritage — saffron-scented rice dishes, slow-cooked lamb, and fish pulled from the warm, shallow waters of the Arabian Gulf.
dish1_desc: Spiced rice cooked with meat or fish in a fragrant broth with dried limes (loomi) and rose water. The national dish of Bahrain.
dish2_desc: Slow-cooked wheat and lamb or chicken, stirred until porridge-smooth. A Ramadan staple and wedding dish — humble, ancient, deeply satisfying.
dish3_desc: Sweet rice cooked with sugar, saffron, and cardamom. Served alongside fish as a rich, fragrant counterpoint.

name: Bangladesh
cuisine_summary: Bangladeshi food is mustard-oil bold and river-fresh — hilsa fish in sharp mustard sauce, rice at every meal, and fiery curries built around the vast delta's endless freshwater catch.
dish1_desc: Hilsa fish marinated in mustard paste and green chile, then steamed in banana leaf. The dish Bangladeshis are most homesick for.
dish2_desc: Hilsa fish cooked in a sharp, pungent mustard sauce with green chiles. Simple, deeply loved, and non-negotiable in Bengali homes.
dish3_desc: Rich beef or mutton biryani from old Dhaka, perfumed with saffron and sour dried plum (aloo bukhara). Sweeter and richer than its Indian cousins.

name: Barbados
cuisine_summary: Bajan food is Caribbean with a British backbone — flying fish, cou-cou, ferocious pepper sauce, and rum cake. The flying fish is practically the national symbol.
dish1_desc: The national dish. Okra-and-cornmeal polenta paired with flying fish in a herbed tomato sauce. Every Barbadian has an opinion on who makes it best.
dish2_desc: Pickled pork with sweet potato pudding, eaten on Saturdays. An island tradition as fixed as the weekend itself.
dish3_desc: Baked macaroni and cheese, Bajan-style — firmer, spiced with mustard and hot sauce, cut into squares. On every Sunday table.

name: Belarus
cuisine_summary: Belarusian food is Eastern European peasant cooking at its most potato-devoted — draniki (potato pancakes), thick beet soups, and pork stews. Filling, warming, and unashamedly starchy.
dish1_desc: Grated potato pancakes fried in oil until the edges are lacy and crisp. Served with sour cream. Belarus's most beloved dish.
dish2_desc: Thick stew of pork ribs and sausage in a rye flour sauce. Served with draniki or blini for mopping — a Sunday feast.
dish3_desc: Cold bright-pink beet soup with cucumber, radish, hard-boiled egg, and sour cream. Refreshing in summer, striking on the table.

name: Belgium
cuisine_summary: Belgian food punches well above its size — arguably the world's best fries, chocolate that sets the global standard, beer-braised beef stew, and mussels eaten by the potful on newspaper-lined tables.
dish1_desc: Mussels steamed open in white wine, butter, and shallots, served with a mountain of double-fried fries. Belgium's defining meal.
dish2_desc: Beef slow-braised in Belgian ale with thyme and bay until sticky and rich. Best eaten with thick-cut bread to catch the sauce.
dish3_desc: Dense, chewy waffles studded with pearl sugar that caramelizes as it bakes. Eaten warm, straight from the iron — no toppings needed.

name: Belize
cuisine_summary: Belizean food is a creole blend of Maya, Garifuna, and Caribbean traditions — rice and beans cooked in coconut milk, stewed chicken, and ceviche made from fish pulled off the barrier reef.
dish1_desc: Kidney beans slow-cooked in coconut milk and folded through rice. The Belizean daily staple — eaten at nearly every meal.
dish2_desc: Garifuna coconut fish stew served with mashed plantain. Rich, slightly sweet, and deeply satisfying — a dish of the coast.
dish3_desc: Fried corn tortillas piled with refried beans, shredded cheese, and pickled cabbage. The Belizean roadside snack.

name: Benin
cuisine_summary: Beninese cuisine is West African cooking at its most elemental — cornmeal and yam porridges anchoring every meal, peanut-based sauces layered with chiles and dried fish, and grilled bonga fish pulled from the lagoon. Acarajé (black-eyed pea fritters fried in palm oil) traveled from Benin to Brazil with the slave trade and became a street-food icon on two continents. Peanuts and peppers are the two constants; palm oil is the medium through which everything is cooked and flavored.
dish1_desc: Stiff cornmeal cooked in a red palm oil and tomato sauce. Rich, deeply spiced, and served with fish or slow-cooked meat.
dish2_desc: Ground peanut paste shaped into balls or sticks and deep-fried until crunchy. The everywhere snack of Benin and the wider region.
dish3_desc: Whole tilapia marinated in chiles and spices, grilled over charcoal. Served with pepper sauce, fried plantain, and cold beer.

name: Bhutan
cuisine_summary: Bhutanese food is fiery and humble — dried red chiles here aren't a seasoning, they're a vegetable. Yak cheese, chiles, and red rice form the holy trinity of a cuisine shaped by altitude and Buddhist tradition.
dish1_desc: Fresh green chiles simmered with soft local yak cheese until melted into a saucy, fiery stew. Bhutan's national dish, eaten daily.
dish2_desc: Pork slow-cooked with dried red chiles and radish. Smoky, deeply spiced, and warming at altitude.
dish3_desc: Nutty, chewy semi-milled red rice grown in the Paro valley. More complex than white rice and the base of every Bhutanese meal.

name: Bolivia
cuisine_summary: Bolivian food is high-altitude hearty — potato stews in countless varieties, marinated grilled meats, and juicy salteñas eaten as a mid-morning snack. Bolivia is the world's most diverse potato country.
dish1_desc: Baked empanada filled with a juicy stew of beef or chicken with olives, egg, and potato. The juice running down your chin when you bite in is a feature, not a flaw.
dish2_desc: Peanut soup with beef, vegetables, and pasta. Thick, nutty, and deeply restorative — Bolivia's answer to cold mountain evenings.
dish3_desc: Breaded, pounded beef cutlet laid over rice and potatoes and topped with a fried egg and fresh salsa. The Cochabamba plate.

name: Bosnia and Herzegovina
cuisine_summary: Bosnian food is grilled meat and Ottoman pastry — hand-rolled phyllo pies, skinless sausages over charcoal, and thick Bosnian coffee served in a džezva with a sugar cube and a piece of Turkish delight.
dish1_desc: Skinless minced beef sausages grilled over charcoal, stuffed into pillowy somun flatbread with raw onion and kajmak cream. Bosnia's great street food.
dish2_desc: Coiled phyllo pastry filled with seasoned minced beef, baked until burnished gold. Breakfast food, late-night food, every-occasion food.
dish3_desc: Layers of beef, lamb, and vegetables sealed in a clay pot and cooked for hours. The slow-cooked Bosnian stew at its most elemental.

name: Botswana
cuisine_summary: Botswanan cuisine is the food of a landlocked, semi-arid country — honest, sustaining, and built on what the land provides. Seswaa is the dish of weddings and ceremonies: beef or goat pounded after slow boiling into rough, shredded strands, served over sorghum or maize pap. Morogo (foraged wild leafy greens) is the everyday vegetable. Sun-dried meat preserves protein through dry seasons. It is food shaped by constraint and community, not abundance — and it carries that directness with quiet dignity.
dish1_desc: Beef or goat slow-boiled until falling apart, then pounded with a wooden pestle and served with pap. The dish of funerals, weddings, and national holidays.
dish2_desc: Thick sorghum or maize porridge eaten with stew, meat, or vegetables. The Botswanan staple — present at every meal.
dish3_desc: Wild leafy greens simmered with onion and tomato. Simple, nutritious, and the everyday vegetable side across the country.

name: Brazil
cuisine_summary: Brazilian food is a continent's worth of cuisines in one country — black bean stew from African traditions, Pampas barbecue from the south, and street food like acarajé from the Afro-Brazilian kitchens of Bahia.
dish1_desc: Black bean stew with pork cuts (ribs, sausage, ears, tail), served with rice, collard greens, farofa, and orange slices. The national dish — Saturday's communal meal.
dish2_desc: Brazilian barbecue: beef, lamb, and pork cuts cooked on long skewers over charcoal and sliced tableside. The rodízio format means it never stops coming.
dish3_desc: Black-eyed pea fritter deep-fried in dendê palm oil and stuffed with shrimp, vatapá paste, and hot sauce. The street food of Bahia.

name: Brunei
cuisine_summary: Bruneian food is Malay at its core — coconut milk curries, rice cooked in bamboo over fire, and ambuyat (sago starch paste) eaten communally by twirling it onto long bamboo forks.
dish1_desc: Glutinous sago starch paste twirled onto a bamboo fork and dipped in a sour, spicy binjai fruit sauce. Brunei's national dish — communal, tactile, and unlike anything else.
dish2_desc: Rice with fried chicken and sambal, wrapped in paper. Brunei's beloved cheap-and-cheerful meal, available at all hours.
dish3_desc: Glutinous rice cooked in turmeric and coconut milk, wrapped tightly in palm leaves. A traditional Bruneian festival snack.

name: Bulgaria
cuisine_summary: Bulgarian food is Balkan peasant cooking with a world-class yogurt culture — slow-roasted meats, stuffed peppers, and the tangy white sirene cheese that turns up in almost everything.
dish1_desc: Flaky filo pastry filled with beaten egg and crumbled sirene cheese, baked until golden. The Bulgarian breakfast — always with yogurt or boza.
dish2_desc: Tomato, cucumber, roasted pepper, and onion piled high and blanketed in grated white cheese. The freshest, simplest thing on any Bulgarian table.
dish3_desc: Pork or chicken slow-cooked with peppers, mushrooms, and onions in a sealed clay pot. Rich, perfectly seasoned, made for cold evenings.

name: Burkina Faso
cuisine_summary: Burkinabé food is West African grain-cooking at its most essential — millet and sorghum porridge with peanut-based sauces, street brochettes over charcoal, and simple soups that feed families on little.
dish1_desc: Stiff millet or sorghum paste eaten by hand, dipped into peanut sauce or baobab leaf sauce. The national staple — present at every meal.
dish2_desc: Rice cooked in a rich broth of meat, tomato, and vegetables until deeply flavored. The celebratory Friday dish.
dish3_desc: Skewered lamb or beef grilled over charcoal at every street corner. Eaten with raw onion, mustard sauce, and bread.

name: Burma (Myanmar)
cuisine_summary: Burmese cuisine sits at the cultural crossroads of India, China, and Southeast Asia — yet tastes like none of them. Lahpet thohk (fermented tea-leaf salad) is unlike anything else on earth: tossed tableside with peanuts, fried garlic, dried shrimp, and tomatoes. Mohinga, the national breakfast, is a catfish-and-lemongrass noodle soup eaten by millions every morning. Ohn-no khao swe (coconut chicken noodles) is comfort food of the highest order. The cuisine rewards curiosity — every dish has layers that reveal themselves slowly.
dish1_desc: Fermented tea leaves tossed tableside with crunchy lentils, peanuts, sesame, cabbage, and lime. The dish to order first.
dish2_desc: Catfish-and-rice-noodle soup with lemongrass. The Burmese breakfast, eaten all day.
dish3_name: Coconut chicken noodle soup (ohn no khao swè)
dish3_desc: Yellow curry coconut broth with egg noodles and chicken. Garnish with fried onions, chile, lime, hard egg.

name: Burundi
cuisine_summary: Burundian cuisine is quietly sustaining — built around the staples that keep a densely populated, landlocked country fed. Beans appear at nearly every meal: red kidney beans in thick sauce are the backbone of daily life. Ugali (stiff maize or sorghum porridge) is served alongside, scooped with the hand. Plantain, sweet potato, and cassava fill the gaps. On special occasions, goat is grilled over charcoal. The cuisine is humble and nourishing — a reflection of a country that grows most of what it eats.
dish1_desc: Pounded cassava leaves cooked in palm oil with onion and sometimes groundnuts. The everyday green stew — nutrient-dense and filling.
dish2_desc: Dried and grilled lake fish from Lake Tanganyika, eaten with ugali. The protein of the inland fishing economy.
dish3_desc: Pumpkin cooked with kidney beans in a savory, lightly spiced stew. A humble and nourishing everyday staple.

name: Cabo Verde
cuisine_summary: Cape Verdean food is Atlantic island cooking with deep Portuguese roots — slow-simmered corn and bean stews, freshly grilled tuna, and cachupa (the national dish) that cooks all day and tastes better the next morning refried.
dish1_desc: Slow-cooked stew of hominy corn, beans, and whatever meat or fish is available. The national dish — eaten for dinner, then fried up crispy for breakfast the next day.
dish2_desc: Fresh tuna or wahoo grilled over charcoal with lemon and local spices. The simplest and most satisfying thing the surrounding ocean offers.
dish3_desc: Clear fish broth with vegetables and cassava. Light, restorative, the everyday soup of the islands.

name: Cambodia
cuisine_summary: Cambodian food is subtle and herb-forward — sour soups fragrant with lemongrass and kaffir lime, coconut-based curry pastes, and fish amok (the national dish) steamed in banana leaf until barely set.
dish1_desc: Freshwater fish in a coconut milk and kroeung (lemongrass paste) curry, steamed in banana leaf until just set. Cambodia's national dish — delicate, fragrant, irreplaceable.
dish2_desc: Grilled pork over broken rice, eaten at breakfast. Simple, lightly smoky, and the Cambodian morning staple.
dish3_desc: Rice noodles in a fresh green fish-based curry sauce with raw vegetables and herbs. The traditional Khmer breakfast noodle.

name: Cameroon
cuisine_summary: Cameroonian food straddles West and Central Africa — peanut stews and grilled fish on the coast, bitter-leaf and palm oil dishes inland, and ndolé (the national dish) that is complex enough to anchor a whole cuisine.
dish1_desc: Bitter leaves stewed with groundnuts, shrimp, and beef or fish. Cameroon's national dish — rich, layered, and unlike anything else in the region.
dish2_desc: Shredded wild fern cooked with waterleaf and palm oil, served with water fufu. A dish of the western highlands, eaten with great ceremony.
dish3_desc: Beef skewers marinated and grilled over charcoal at every roadside. Eaten with fried plantain and a hot pepper sauce.

name: Canada
cuisine_summary: Canadian food is regional and quietly underrated — Québécois poutine and tourtière, Maritime seafood, Indigenous bannock and bison, and urban food scenes shaped by waves of immigration. The country is too large for a single cuisine.
dish1_desc: French fries topped with fresh cheese curds and hot brown gravy. Québec's greatest export — comfort food perfected and endlessly riffed on.
dish2_desc: Flaky pastry shells filled with a gooey, runny butter-sugar-egg filling. Canada's most distinctly national dessert, debated endlessly (raisins or no raisins).
dish3_desc: Spiced pork and beef double-crust pie from Québec, eaten at Christmas and New Year's. Warm, deeply savory, and tied to family tradition.

name: Central African Republic
cuisine_summary: Central African food is forest-to-table — cassava in every form, smoked and dried bush meat, greens cooked in palm oil, and groundnut-based stews. Simple, sustaining, shaped by the equatorial rainforest.
dish1_desc: Pounded cassava paste (fufu) eaten by hand and dipped into stews and sauces. The foundational daily staple of the CAR.
dish2_desc: Spiced meatballs in a peanut-and-tomato sauce, served over rice or with cassava. A festive dish reserved for celebrations.
dish3_desc: Smoked or dried fish slow-cooked with greens in palm oil. The everyday protein dish across the country.

name: Chad
cuisine_summary: Chadian food is Saharan and Sahelian — millet and sorghum porridges, dried fish from Lake Chad, and lamb stews seasoned with spices carried along trans-Saharan trade routes.
dish1_desc: Stiff millet or sorghum porridge rolled into balls and eaten by hand, dipped into soup or sauce. The Chadian daily staple.
dish2_desc: Thick stew of okra, peanuts, tomatoes, and dried fish or meat. Earthy, filling, and the most common sauce eaten over boule.
dish3_desc: Sun-dried and smoked small fish from Lake Chad. An essential regional protein, traded across the Sahel for centuries.

name: Chile
cuisine_summary: Chilean cuisine runs the length of one of the world's most geographically extreme countries — 4,300 kilometers of Pacific coastline, Atacama desert, Patagonian steppe, and Andean mountain. The sea defines the table: congrio (king crab), piure (sea squirt), and locos (abalone) are national obsessions. Inland: pastel de choclo (a corn-and-meat casserole), cazuela (slow broth with vegetables and beef), and empanadas from clay ovens. The Maipo and Casablanca valleys produce world-class Carménère and Sauvignon Blanc. Chilean food is not loud — it lets extraordinary raw ingredients speak quietly.
dish1_desc: Ground beef, chicken, olives, hard-boiled egg, and raisins topped with a sweet corn crust and baked in a clay bowl. Chile's great comfort dish.
dish2_desc: Clear broth with beef or chicken, potato, corn on the cob, squash, and rice. The everyday Chilean soup — clean, nourishing, unpretentious.
dish3_desc: Oven-baked pastry filled with spiced ground beef, onion, olive, egg, and raisin. The classic Chilean empanada — juicy inside, golden outside.

name: China
cuisine_summary: San Francisco's Chinatown — established in 1848 — is the oldest in North America and the birthplace of American-Chinese food as we know it. Dishes like chop suey and egg foo yung were invented here and spread across the country. Cecilia Chiang's Mandarin Restaurant introduced authentic regional Chinese cuisine to American diners in 1961. Today, SF's Chinese food scene spans Cantonese dim sum in Chinatown, hand-pulled Sichuan noodles in the Richmond, and some of the country's finest Hong Kong-style seafood — a 175-year culinary legacy still very much alive.
dish1_desc: Shanghai soup dumplings — bite the side, sip the broth, then eat the rest. Don't burn yourself.
dish2_desc: Silken tofu in a numbing chile-bean sauce with ground pork. Sichuan's calling card.
dish3_desc: Thin wheat noodles in spicy sesame-chile sauce with crispy pork. Mix before eating.

name: Colombia
cuisine_summary: Colombian food is regional and hearty — Bogotá ajiaco, coastal seafood rice, and deep-fried street food. Arepas (corn cakes) are the constant — eaten at breakfast, lunch, dinner, and any moment in between.
dish1_desc: Thick soup of three varieties of potato, chicken, corn, and guasca herb. Bogotá's defining dish — warming, complex, unlike any other potato soup.
dish2_desc: The Antioquia mega-plate: beans, rice, chicharrón, chorizo, fried egg, avocado, fried plantain, and arepa. Not a meal — a statement.
dish3_desc: Grilled or fried corn cake eaten at every meal. Plain, stuffed with cheese, smeared with butter — the backbone of Colombian daily eating.

name: Comoros
cuisine_summary: Comorian food is Indian Ocean island cooking — coconut milk rice, spiced meats, and the layered influence of Arab, Swahili, and French traders who passed through these perfume islands for centuries.
dish1_desc: Spiced rice cooked with goat meat and warm spices — cinnamon, cardamom, cloves. Swahili-influenced, fragrant, and the dish of celebrations.
dish2_desc: Coconut bread cooked on a griddle until golden. The Comorian morning staple — slightly sweet, eaten with tea.
dish3_desc: Fresh rock lobster grilled and served with a coconut-spiced sauce. The island's prized seafood, pulled straight from the Indian Ocean.

name: Congo (Dem. Rep.)
cuisine_summary: DRC food spans the continent's largest country — cassava, plantain, and palm oil underpin everything, with smoked fish, grilled meats, and profound regional variation from the forest to the savanna.
dish1_desc: Dense cassava paste rolled into balls and dipped into sauce or stew. The DRC daily staple — eaten by hand, always with something bold alongside.
dish2_desc: Chicken in a thick palm nut sauce. The national dish — oily, earthy, and deeply flavored by the palm fruit.
dish3_desc: Cassava leaves pounded and cooked in palm oil with onion and dried fish. The green stew present at every DRC table.

name: Congo (Republic of)
cuisine_summary: Congolese (Republic) food is equatorial forest cooking — cassava is the backbone, palm oil is the fat, and freshwater fish and smoked meats are the proteins. Saka-saka (cassava leaf stew) is on every table.
dish1_desc: Pounded cassava leaves slow-cooked in palm oil with garlic and onion. The most beloved everyday dish — deeply green, rich, and filling.
dish2_desc: Chicken simmered in palm butter sauce with garlic and chile. Central Africa's great chicken dish, rich with the taste of the forest.
dish3_desc: Fish wrapped tightly in banana leaves with spices and cooked over charcoal. The river fisherman's method — smoky and self-contained.

name: Costa Rica
cuisine_summary: Costa Rican food is 'pura vida' on a plate — simple, fresh, and completely unpretentious. Gallo pinto at breakfast every single morning, and a cuisine that doesn't shout but consistently satisfies.
dish1_desc: Black beans and rice fried together with Lizano sauce, onion, and bell pepper. Costa Rica's national breakfast — eaten every morning without exception.
dish2_desc: The weekday lunch plate: rice, black beans, fried sweet plantain, salad, and a protein. The working Costa Rican's daily meal.
dish3_desc: Beef and vegetable soup with yuca, plantain, corn on the cob, and chayote. The Sunday family soup, made slowly and eaten communally.

name: Croatia
cuisine_summary: Croatian food is two cuisines split by mountains — Adriatic seafood and olive oil on the coast, hearty Austro-Hungarian meat stews and pastries inland. Both sides are worth the trip.
dish1_desc: Lamb or octopus slow-cooked under a bell-shaped iron lid buried in embers. The Croatian feast dish — smoky, impossibly tender, worth the hours.
dish2_desc: Fisherman's stew of multiple fish types with tomatoes, wine, and herbs, eaten with creamy polenta. The Dalmatian coast's defining dish.
dish3_desc: Pasta dough stuffed with cottage cheese and sour cream, boiled or baked. Zagreb's comfort food — a Croatian cultural heritage dish.

name: Cuba
cuisine_summary: Cuban food is slow-cooked and satisfying — black beans, braised pork, and fried sweet plantain at the center of nearly every plate. The Cuban sandwich took its form here before it conquered the world.
dish1_desc: Shredded beef braised long and slow in tomato sauce with peppers and onion. Cuba's national dish — the name means 'old clothes,' which tells you nothing about how good it tastes.
dish2_desc: Black beans and white rice cooked together until the rice turns smoky and dark. The foundational Cuban side, named for the Moors and Christians of Spanish history.
dish3_desc: Whole pig marinated in mojo (sour orange and garlic) and roasted over an open pit. The centerpiece of every Cuban celebration.

name: Cyprus
cuisine_summary: Cypriot food is Eastern Mediterranean mezze — grilled meats, charred halloumi, and slow-cooked lamb from clay pots. The island sits between Greek and Middle Eastern cooking and borrows freely from both.
dish1_desc: Semi-hard brined sheep's milk cheese grilled or fried until golden outside and squeaky within. Cyprus's great gift to the world's breakfast tables and barbecues.
dish2_desc: Large chunks of lamb or pork slow-roasted on a long skewer over charcoal for hours. The Cypriot Sunday ritual — unhurried, sociable, deeply satisfying.
dish3_desc: Lamb or pork layered with onion, tomato, and cumin in a sealed clay pot, baked slowly until tender. Village cooking at its most essential.

name: Czechia
cuisine_summary: Czech food is beer-hall hearty — roast pork with bread dumplings and sauerkraut, goulash ladled into bread bowls, and svíčková (braised beef in cream sauce) that takes an afternoon to make properly.
dish1_desc: Braised beef sirloin in a creamy root vegetable sauce, served with bread dumplings, cranberry, and whipped cream. The Czech Sunday dish — rich, patient, and much-loved.
dish2_desc: Roast pork with bread dumplings and braised sauerkraut. The Czech pub classic — demanding a cold Pilsner alongside.
dish3_desc: Dough spiraled around a cylinder, grilled over charcoal, and rolled in cinnamon sugar. Prague's beloved street pastry, warm and fragrant.

name: Denmark
cuisine_summary: Danish food is New Nordic and old smørrebrød in one — open-faced rye bread sandwiches piled high with pickled herring or smoked salmon, and a modern restaurant scene that put foraging and fermentation on the world map.
dish1_desc: Open-faced rye bread sandwiches topped with pickled herring, smoked salmon, liver pâté, or roast beef, decorated with surgical care. The Danish lunch, eaten with aquavit.
dish2_desc: Pan-fried pork-and-veal meatballs served with potato salad and pickled beets. The Danish home-cooking staple — satisfying, never fussy.
dish3_desc: Fluffy spherical pancake balls dusted with powdered sugar and dipped in jam. The Christmas-season street snack and cozy kitchen tradition.

name: Djibouti
cuisine_summary: Djiboutian food reflects its position at the Horn of Africa's trade crossroads — Somali and Ethiopian cooking form the base, layered with Yemeni spice traditions and French baguettes from the colonial era.
dish1_desc: Spiced rice with lamb or goat cooked with cumin, cardamom, and lime. Djibouti's version of the Gulf's fragrant rice dish.
dish2_desc: Spongy, lightly sour fermented flatbread — similar to Ethiopian injera. Eaten with honey at breakfast or used to scoop stews.
dish3_desc: Spiced goat soup with vegetables and chiles. The street-food staple and everyday restorative dish.

name: Dominica
cuisine_summary: Dominican (Dominica) food is Creole cooking rooted in African and French heritage, shaped by one of the Caribbean's most untouched natural landscapes. Mountain chicken (the giant frog crapaud), freshwater crayfish, and dasheen (taro) are local staples found nowhere else in quite the same form. Callaloo soup, fish broth, and provisions (root vegetables) are everyday anchors. The 'Nature Isle' grows most of what it eats — spices, cocoa, bananas, and citrus from volcanic soil that produces some of the Caribbean's most intensely flavored produce.
dish1_desc: Dasheen (taro) leaves blended into a thick, dark green soup with coconut milk and okra. The Caribbean island staple — rich, earthy, deeply nourishing.
dish2_desc: Rice cooked with pigeon peas, coconut milk, and chicken or pork. One-pot Caribbean cooking at its most comforting.
dish3_desc: Salt cod sautéed with onion, tomato, and peppers, served with fried ripe plantain. The everyday island breakfast plate.

name: Dominican Republic
cuisine_summary: Dominican food is hearty, colorful, and proudly filling — slow-braised meats, rice, beans, and plantain in every form. La bandera (the flag plate) is the national midday meal and the anchor of daily life.
dish1_desc: White rice, stewed red beans, and braised chicken or beef — the national lunch plate, eaten across the country every single day.
dish2_desc: Mashed boiled green plantain served with sautéed red onions, fried white cheese, salami, and eggs. The Dominican breakfast.
dish3_desc: Seven-meat stew with root vegetables, corn, and herbs, simmered for hours. The ultimate Dominican celebration dish.

name: Ecuador
cuisine_summary: Ecuadorian food spans three entirely different landscapes — ceviche and seafood on the Pacific coast, potato-and-cheese soups in the Andean highlands, and jungle ingredients from the Amazon. Each region eats as if the others don't exist.
dish1_desc: Shrimp cured in citrus with tomato, onion, and cilantro, served with plantain chips and popcorn on the side. The coast's essential dish.
dish2_desc: Thick potato and cheese soup finished with avocado slices. The Andean highlands' comfort dish — warming, creamy, and filling at altitude.
dish3_desc: Chicken braised in naranjilla fruit juice, beer, and spices until deeply flavored. Ecuador's beloved everyday stew, served over rice.

name: Egypt
cuisine_summary: Egyptian food is ancient and filling — slow-cooked lentil dishes, falafel eaten warm in flatbread, and koshari (Cairo's great street food) that layers rice, pasta, and lentils into something improbably delicious.
dish1_desc: Cairo's definitive street food: rice, pasta, and lentils layered in a bowl and topped with spiced tomato sauce and a mountain of crispy fried onions. Vegetarian, cheap, and addictive.
dish2_desc: Slow-cooked fava beans mashed with lemon, garlic, and cumin. Egypt's breakfast for thousands of years — served with eggs, bread, and a lot of olive oil.
dish3_desc: Jute leaves cooked into a thick, slightly viscous green soup with garlic and coriander, poured over rice or eaten with flatbread and rabbit or chicken.

name: El Salvador
cuisine_summary: Salvadoran food is built around masa — and its greatest expression is the pupusa: a thick handmade corn cake stuffed with cheese, chicharrón, or loroco flower, pressed flat and griddled, then buried under curtido (fermented cabbage slaw) and tomato salsa. Beyond pupusas: yuca frita with chicharrón, sopa de pata (cow's foot soup), and tamales wrapped in banana leaf for Sunday mornings. The cuisine is unpretentious, immediate, and made for sharing — El Salvador's most beloved dishes all began as street food.
dish1_desc: Thick handmade corn tortillas stuffed with cheese, refried beans, or chicharrón, cooked on a dry griddle. El Salvador's national dish, eaten at breakfast, lunch, and dinner.
dish2_desc: Lightly fermented cabbage slaw with carrot, onion, and oregano. The required and essential accompaniment to every pupusa — crunchy, sour, non-negotiable.
dish3_desc: Cow's foot soup with vegetables, corn, tripe, and herbs. A slow-cooked weekend ritual considered deeply restorative.

name: Equatorial Guinea
cuisine_summary: Equatorial Guinean food is Central African rainforest cooking with a Spanish colonial overlay — cassava, plantain, and forest meats in the interior; rice and fresh seafood on the coast.
dish1_desc: Spiced broth with goat or fish and local hot peppers. The all-occasion dish, eaten for every celebration and as an everyday comfort.
dish2_desc: Peanut soup with chicken and vegetables — a Spanish-influenced adaptation of the West African groundnut stew.
dish3_desc: Malanga (taro) cooked with beans and palm oil. A simple, starchy staple of the inland Bioko diet.

name: Eritrea
cuisine_summary: Eritrean food shares much with Ethiopian — injera flatbread with spiced stews — but carries its own Red Sea coastal influence, an Italian pasta legacy from colonialism, and spice blends distinctly its own.
dish1_desc: Spiced beef stew cooked with berbere chile paste, slow and red. Eritrea's signature meat dish — bold, aromatic, and inseparable from injera.
dish2_desc: Chickpea or broad bean flour sauce slow-cooked into a thick, warming stew. The everyday Eritrean vegetarian staple — eaten with injera at every meal.
dish3_desc: Spongy sourdough flatbread laid out as both plate and utensil, piled with various stews (tsebhi). The foundation and vessel of every Eritrean meal.

name: Estonia
cuisine_summary: Estonian food is Baltic and quietly Nordic — dark rye bread, cold-smoked fish, blood sausage, and berry-picking culture. The cuisine is rooted in the forest and the sea, with a Soviet dairy-and-potato layer underneath.
dish1_desc: Barley and potato porridge cooked slowly with pork fat, served with sour cream. Ancient Estonian peasant food — still proudly eaten and deeply warming.
dish2_desc: Blood sausage with barley filling, baked and served with lingonberry jam and sour cream. Estonia's traditional Christmas dish — earthy and essential.
dish3_desc: Baltic sprats cold-smoked and served on buttered dark rye bread. The Estonian pantry staple — salty, oily, perfect with a beer.

name: Eswatini
cuisine_summary: Swazi cuisine is rooted in the rhythms of the land — maize is the backbone, pounded into pap (thick porridge) and eaten with slow-stewed meats and imifino (foraged wild greens). Emasi (soured milk) is a dietary staple and a point of cultural pride. Umncweba (sun-dried meat, similar to biltong) preserves protein through dry seasons. Traditional Swazi food is shaped by subsistence farming and communal life — meals are simple, generous, and closely tied to the agricultural calendar and ancestral tradition.
dish1_desc: Soured thick milk, similar to a chunky yogurt. Eaten with pap or on its own — the Swazi daily staple, sharp and cooling.
dish2_desc: Pumpkin porridge thickened with mealie meal. A traditional Swazi breakfast dish — slightly sweet, warming, and comforting.
dish3_desc: Dried, salted strips of beef similar to biltong. The Swazi method of preserving meat — intensely savory and chewy.

name: Ethiopia
cuisine_summary: Ethiopian cuisine is one of the world's great communal eating traditions. At its center is injera — a large, spongy sourdough flatbread made from teff, spread with wats (slow-simmered stews) of lentils, chickpeas, lamb, or beef, spiced with berbere and mitmita. You eat with your hands, tearing injera to scoop up the stews. Fasting traditions in the Ethiopian Orthodox Church have produced one of the world's most sophisticated vegetarian and vegan cuisines — misir wat, gomen, and shiro are remarkable without a scrap of meat. Coffee originated in Ethiopia, and the coffee ceremony — three rounds, hours long — is as important as any dish on the table.
dish1_desc: Chicken stew with berbere spice and hard-boiled egg, scooped with injera. The Sunday dish.
dish2_desc: Beef or lamb sautéed with onion, peppers, and rosemary. Crispy edges, tender center.
dish3_desc: Hand-minced raw beef seasoned with mitmita spice and clarified spiced butter. Eat with injera and ayib (mild cheese).

name: Fiji
cuisine_summary: Fijian food is Pacific island cooking layered with Indian and Chinese influences brought by colonial-era laborers — coconut milk seafood dishes, earth oven feasts, and curry that has been Fijian for generations.
dish1_desc: Raw fish 'cooked' in citrus juice then mixed with coconut cream, chiles, and onion. Fiji's ceviche — bright, tropical, and the first thing to order.
dish2_desc: Meats and root vegetables wrapped in banana leaves and slow-cooked in an underground earth oven. The Fijian feast method for weddings, funerals, and celebrations.
dish3_desc: Taro leaves simmered in coconut milk with onion and spices. The everyday green vegetable dish of the islands.

name: Finland
cuisine_summary: Finnish food is forest and lake — reindeer, foraged mushrooms and cloudberries, rye bread dark enough to outlast civilization, and smoked fish from a thousand lakes. Simple, seasonal, and quietly excellent.
dish1_desc: Thin rye pastry shells filled with rice or potato porridge, eaten spread with egg butter. The Karelian pasty — Finland's most iconic baked good.
dish2_desc: Creamy salmon and potato soup with dill and a touch of leek. The Finnish lake-country comfort dish, year-round.
dish3_desc: Thinly sliced reindeer sautéed in butter, served with mashed potato and lingonberry jam. Lapland on a plate.

name: France
cuisine_summary: French cuisine is the foundation on which most of Western professional cooking was built — the brigade system, the mother sauces, the philosophy that cooking is an art worth a lifetime of discipline. Regionally it is vast: Brittany's butter and buckwheat crêpes, Provence's olive oil and tomatoes, Lyon's offal and quenelles (the city Bocuse called the world's greatest food capital), Alsace's choucroute and Riesling-braised pork, Bordeaux's wine-country simplicity. The baguette, the bistro, the tasting menu — all French inventions. Haute cuisine and the corner boulangerie are equally serious. France doesn't just have a cuisine; it has a philosophy of eating that shaped the entire world's table.
dish1_desc: Grilled steak with crispy fries — the bistro lunch staple. Order it medium-rare.
dish2_desc: Open-faced ham and gruyère sandwich, finished under the broiler with béchamel.
dish3_desc: Vanilla custard with a torched sugar crust you crack with the back of a spoon.

name: Gabon
cuisine_summary: Gabonese food is equatorial coast and rainforest — fresh Atlantic seafood in Libreville, smoked fish and bush meat inland, and everything enriched with red palm oil and pounded peanuts.
dish1_desc: Chicken braised in palm nut sauce until rich and deeply orange. Gabon's national dish — oily, earthy, and inseparable from rice.
dish2_desc: Whole fish marinated in piri piri and herbs, grilled over charcoal. The Libreville street-food staple, eaten with fried plantain.
dish3_desc: Roasted pumpkin seed paste cooked with fish or chicken and leafy greens. A traditional dish of the interior forest communities.

name: Gambia
cuisine_summary: Gambian food is West African simplicity centered on rice — cooked in groundnut sauce, palm oil, or tomato broth, with fresh fish from the river and Atlantic coast. The groundnut stew is a national institution.
dish1_desc: Rice cooked in a rich tomato-and-meat broth with vegetables and fish in one pot. The Gambian jollof — every family has a version they'll defend.
dish2_desc: Thick groundnut stew with beef or chicken and sweet potato. Rich, peanut-forward, and deeply satisfying — eaten at every gathering.
dish3_desc: Chicken or fish marinated in lemon juice and mustard, braised low and slow with mountains of caramelized onions. Beloved across West Africa.

name: Georgia
cuisine_summary: Georgian food is walnut-rich and wine-ancient — cheese-filled bread boats, soup dumplings eaten with ritual, and the supra feast tradition where a tamada (toastmaster) guides hours of toasts and food.
dish1_desc: Bread boat filled with melted sulguni cheese and a runny egg cracked in at the end. Tear the edges, stir everything together, drag through the filling.
dish2_desc: Large pleated soup dumplings filled with spiced pork and beef. Bite the knot, sip the hot broth inside first, eat the rest. The knot is left on the plate.
dish3_desc: Poached chicken blanketed in a cold walnut sauce with fenugreek, coriander, and garlic. Served at room temperature — the Georgian holiday centerpiece.

name: Germany
cuisine_summary: German food is regional and more varied than its reputation — Bavaria has pork knuckle and pretzels, the north has herring and smoked eel, and Berlin has currywurst from a snack stand at midnight. Beer is always contextually correct.
dish1_desc: Beef marinated for days in vinegar and aromatics, then braised until fork-tender. Germany's national pot roast — served with red cabbage and potato dumplings.
dish2_desc: Slow-roasted pork knuckle with shatteringly crisp crackling, served with sauerkraut and mustard. Bavaria's great beer-hall dish.
dish3_desc: Sliced pork sausage in a curry-spiced ketchup sauce, served with fries or a bread roll. Berlin's beloved street food — simple, satisfying, and eaten standing up.

name: Ghana
cuisine_summary: Ghanaian food is West African cooking at its most vibrant — jollof rice that wins every argument, peanut soups with fufu pounded tableside, fermented fish for depth, and kelewele spiced plantain from every corner stall.
dish1_desc: Rice cooked in a smoky, spiced tomato-and-pepper base. Ghana insists its version beats Nigeria's. The debate is ongoing and extremely serious.
dish2_desc: Rich peanut broth with chicken or goat, eaten with pounded fufu. The go-to Sunday dish — deep, warming, made with patience.
dish3_desc: Diced ripe plantain fried with ginger, chile, and spices until the outside caramelizes. Accra's irresistible street snack.

name: Greece
cuisine_summary: Greek food is olive oil, lemon, and time — slow-roasted lamb, charred octopus on harbor walls, and mezze that expands every time you think you're finished. The rule is: eat slowly and order more wine.
dish1_desc: Layers of spiced lamb, eggplant, and potato topped with thick béchamel and baked golden. The Greek kitchen's most ambitious and rewarding dish.
dish2_desc: Marinated pork or chicken grilled on skewers, stuffed into pita with tzatziki, tomato, and onion. Fast food executed with dignity.
dish3_desc: Flaky phyllo pastry packed with spinach, feta, and dill. At every Greek table, every celebration, every grandmother's kitchen.

name: Grenada
cuisine_summary: Grenadian food is the Spice Isle on a plate — nutmeg, mace, cloves, and cinnamon season nearly everything. Oil down (the national dish) is a slow coconut milk stew eaten communally, ideally outdoors.
dish1_desc: Breadfruit, salted meat, callaloo, and dumplings slow-cooked in coconut milk until the liquid is fully absorbed. Grenada's national dish — communal, unhurried, fragrant with spice.
dish2_desc: Dasheen leaves simmered and blended with coconut milk, okra, and crab. Lush, dark green, and deeply nourishing.
dish3_desc: Vanilla ice cream churned with fresh Grenadian nutmeg. The island's most beloved dessert — benefiting from the world's finest supply.

name: Guatemala
cuisine_summary: Guatemalan food is ancient Maya cuisine in daily use — corn-based tamales, seed-thickened stews, and pepián (the national dish) made from roasted seeds and chiles whose recipe predates the Spanish arrival by centuries.
dish1_desc: Thick stew of chicken or beef in a sauce of roasted pumpkin seeds, sesame, dried chiles, and tomatoes. Guatemala's national dish — pre-Columbian, complex, extraordinary.
dish2_desc: Corn masa filled with pork and a tomato-chile sauce, wrapped in banana leaves and steamed. The Christmas and celebration food.
dish3_desc: Turkey soup seasoned with dried chiles, achiote, and fresh coriander. An ancient Q'eqchi' Maya ceremonial dish, still served at festivals.

name: Guinea
cuisine_summary: Guinean cuisine is shaped by the country's three distinct regions — the coastal Basse-Côte, the Fouta Djallon highlands, and the savanna interior. Rice is the universal constant, but how it's served shifts: with peanut-based sauces (maafe) in the interior, with palm oil and smoked fish on the coast. Soups built on okra, dried fish, and leafy greens are everyday staples. Fouta Djallon is known for its dairy tradition — a rarity in West Africa. The cuisine is honest and ingredient-driven, built by a country that grows some of the region's finest rice, pineapples, and mangoes.
dish1_desc: Chicken marinated in lemon and mustard, braised with masses of softened onions. Shared across the West African coast, but mastered throughout Guinea.
dish2_desc: Rice cooked long and slowly in a broth of meat, tomato, and vegetables until every grain is deeply flavored. The celebration and everyday meal alike.
dish3_desc: Cassava leaf sauce cooked down with palm oil, dried fish, and spices until thick and dark. The essential green sauce, eaten over rice across the country.

name: Guinea-Bissau
cuisine_summary: Guinea-Bissauan food is West African coastal — rice and fish-based, shaped by the mangrove coast, and with cashew (the country's main export) appearing as a snack and an ingredient throughout.
dish1_desc: Peanut stew with chicken or fish, palm oil, onion, and garlic. The national staple dish — rich, thick, and quietly satisfying.
dish2_desc: Cassava flour stirred into a seasoned fish broth to form a thick porridge. Eaten with grilled fish along the coast — the fisherman's daily meal.
dish3_desc: Rice cooked in tomato and pepper sauce with fish or meat. The West African constant, Guinea-Bissauan style.

name: Guyana
cuisine_summary: Guyanese food is South America's most Caribbean — Indian, African, Chinese, and Amerindian influences creating a unique mix where curry sits next to pepperpot, and roti shares the table with cook-up rice.
dish1_desc: Dark, slow-cooked beef stew made with cassareep (cassava extract), cinnamon, and scotch bonnet. The Amerindian-origin national dish, eaten on Christmas morning.
dish2_desc: Flaky oil-layered flatbread (a legacy of Indian indenture) eaten with potato, goat, or duck curry. The everyday Guyanese meal.
dish3_desc: Rice, black-eyed peas, and meat slow-cooked together in coconut milk. The Guyanese one-pot dish — casual, filling, made on Saturdays.

name: Haiti
cuisine_summary: Haitian food is African cooking refracted through French colonialism — slow-braised meats in sour orange marinade, rice and beans in every form, and griot (crispy fried pork) that is the country's most celebrated dish.
dish1_desc: Pork marinated in sour orange and epis spice paste, braised until tender then deep-fried until crackling-crisp. Haiti's most beloved dish — eaten with pikliz (fiery pickled slaw) on the side.
dish2_desc: Rice and kidney beans or black beans slow-cooked together. The Haitian daily staple — inseparable from every main course on every table.
dish3_desc: Pumpkin and beef soup with pasta, root vegetables, and warm spices. Eaten every January 1st to celebrate Haitian independence — one of the world's most politically charged dishes.

name: Honduras
cuisine_summary: Honduran cuisine is Central American cooking with its own confident identity. The baleada is the great national street food — a thick flour tortilla folded over refried beans, crema, and salty cheese, eaten at any hour. Sopa de caracol (conch soup with coconut milk and yuca) is the Caribbean coast's signature dish, complex and warming. Tapado (a seafood and plantain stew) reflects the Garífuna community's African and Caribbean heritage. From the Pacific to the Caribbean, Honduras has two coastlines and a rich interior of corn, beans, and tropical fruit — a cuisine that rewards more attention than it typically receives.
dish1_desc: Thick flour tortilla filled with refried beans, crumbled white cheese, and cream. Honduras's defining street food — simple, filling, eaten morning to night.
dish2_desc: Conch soup with coconut milk, yuca, and plantain. The Caribbean coast's signature dish — rich, subtly sweet, and deeply satisfying.
dish3_desc: Whole seafood stewed in coconut milk with green plantain and root vegetables. A Garifuna-origin dish from the Caribbean shore — complex and coastal.

name: Hungary
cuisine_summary: Hungarian food is paprika and patience — slow-braised meats, a fish soup that runs red from the spice, and pastries that hint at the empire this cuisine once fed. Gulyás here is a stew, not the watered-down soup the world calls goulash.
dish1_desc: Beef and onion stew deeply seasoned with sweet Hungarian paprika and caraway, simmered until brick-red and thick. The national dish — a stew, emphatically not a soup.
dish2_desc: Pork-stuffed cabbage rolls braised in tomato sauce with sour cream. Slow-cooked, rich, and the definitive Hungarian Sunday family dish.
dish3_desc: Deep-fried dough topped with sour cream and grated cheese. Hungary's great street food — crispy outside, yielding within, impossible to eat neatly.

name: Iceland
cuisine_summary: Icelandic food is Arctic and ocean-driven — lamb that grazes on wild herbs all summer, Atlantic cod and Arctic char, skyr eaten for a thousand years, and a hot dog stand in Reykjavík that is genuinely worth the queue.
dish1_desc: Slow-cooked Icelandic lamb soup with root vegetables and herbs. The national comfort dish — made from some of the world's most flavorful, free-ranging lamb.
dish2_desc: Thick, tangy cultured dairy with the texture of Greek yogurt and more protein. Eaten with berries and cream — Iceland's ancient superfood, now sold globally.
dish3_desc: Icelandic lamb hot dog with crispy fried onion, raw onion, mustard, ketchup, and remoulade. The Bæjarins Beztu stand in Reykjavík has served these since 1937. Bill Clinton had one.

name: India
cuisine_summary: Indian cuisine is one of the world's most vast and varied — not a single cuisine at all, but a mosaic of regional traditions as different from each other as French is from Greek. The north is tandoor-charred bread, slow-cooked kormas, and buttery dal; the south is crispy fermented dosa, coconut-based curries, and tamarind-soured rice; the west is Goan pork vindaloo from the Portuguese era and Gujarati vegetarian cooking of extraordinary refinement; the east is mustard-oil fish from Bengal and dumplings from the Himalayan borderlands. Spice blends, cooking fats, and staple grains shift every few hundred kilometers. India has been shaping global food — through the spice trade alone — for over two thousand years.
dish1_desc: Yogurt-marinated chicken in a tomato-cream sauce. Brit-Indian classic, weeknight favorite.
dish2_desc: Thin, crispy rice-and-lentil crepe wrapped around spiced potato. Eat with sambar and coconut chutney.
dish3_desc: Long-grain basmati rice layered with marinated meat, saffron, and fried onion. Special-occasion food.

name: Indonesia
cuisine_summary: Indonesian food is the world's largest archipelago on a plate — 17,000 islands, 300 ethnic groups, and a cuisine ranging from Balinese pork to Acehnese beef curry, unified by rice, sambal, and coconut milk.
dish1_desc: Fried rice with kecap manis (sweet soy sauce), shallots, and a fried egg on top. Indonesia's national dish — made in a screaming-hot wok with yesterday's rice.
dish2_desc: Beef slow-cooked for hours in coconut milk and spice paste until nearly dry and deeply caramelized. West Sumatran in origin — repeatedly voted the world's best dish.
dish3_desc: Skewered and grilled meat served with peanut sauce and compressed rice cake. The street food that spread across Southeast Asia and then the world.

name: Iran
cuisine_summary: Iranian food is the world's most underrated — long-simmered stews with pomegranate and walnut, saffron-perfumed rice with a golden crispy tahdig crust, and herb-heavy dishes that use fresh herbs by the fistful.
dish1_desc: Herb stew of fenugreek, parsley, and dried fenugreek with kidney beans, dried limes, and lamb. Iran's most beloved dish — slow, sour, and deeply fragrant.
dish2_desc: Perfectly steamed basmati rice with a golden, crispy crust at the bottom of the pot. The most fought-over portion of any Persian meal — the cook's proudest achievement.
dish3_desc: Duck or chicken braised in a dark pomegranate molasses and walnut sauce. Sweet, sour, richly complex — the dish of Nowruz and celebration tables.

name: Iraq
cuisine_summary: Iraqi food is ancient Mesopotamian cooking — slow-cooked lamb and rice dishes, flatbreads from clay ovens, and masgouf (grilled river fish) that has been eaten on the banks of the Tigris for millennia.
dish1_desc: Whole carp split open, marinated in tamarind and spices, and slow-grilled open-faced over an open fire. Iraq's national dish — ancient, smoky, eaten on the Tigris riverbank.
dish2_desc: Whole slow-roasted lamb on a bed of saffron rice with raisins and almonds. The Iraqi dish of feasts and celebrations — fragrant, generous, communal.
dish3_desc: Lamb and vegetable stew poured over broken flatbread (samoon) to soak up the broth. Comfort food at its most elemental — the bread dissolves, the flavor doesn't.

name: Ireland
cuisine_summary: Irish food has had a quiet renaissance — farm-fresh butter and cheese, Atlantic seafood, soda bread warm from the oven, and a pub stew culture that never went out of fashion. The potato's reputation was earned here.
dish1_desc: Lamb or mutton with potato, onion, and carrot, slow-cooked until the broth turns silky and the meat falls apart. Simple, warming, and perfectly suited to the Irish climate.
dish2_desc: Soft, slightly dense bread leavened with baking soda and buttermilk. Best eaten still warm with a thick spread of salted Irish butter — no toasting required.
dish3_desc: Back rashers, pork sausages, black and white pudding, fried eggs, grilled tomato, and soda bread. The morning spread that makes lunch unnecessary.

name: Israel
cuisine_summary: Israeli cuisine is a living archive of Jewish diaspora cooking merged with the flavors of the broader Middle East. Hummus is eaten daily and argued about seriously — the best shops have lines before they open. Shakshuka (eggs poached in spiced tomato) is the morning standard; falafel in warm pita with pickles and tahini is lunch. Yemenite, Moroccan, Persian, and Ashkenazi traditions all share the same table. The modern Israeli food scene — fueled in part by chefs like Yotam Ottolenghi — has made this one of the most globally influential cuisines of the past two decades.
dish1_desc: Warm, mounded chickpea purée with olive oil, sometimes meat or whole chickpeas on top. Eaten with pita, not as a dip.
dish2_desc: Pita stuffed with fried eggplant, hard-boiled egg, hummus, tahini, amba (mango pickle), and herbs.
dish3_desc: Eggs poached in spiced tomato-pepper sauce. Breakfast for two, eaten straight from the pan with bread.

name: Italy
cuisine_summary: Italian immigrants from Genoa and southern Italy began flooding into North Beach in the 1870s, drawn by the Bay and the fishing trade. By 1900, Columbus Avenue was wall-to-wall Italian restaurants. Molinari & Sons deli has been hand-curing salami on Columbus since 1896. Liguria Bakery has baked focaccia the same way since 1911. Caffè Trieste, opened in 1956, was the West Coast's first espresso bar. North Beach — SF's Little Italy — remains one of the most intact Italian-American neighborhoods in the country, where a 150-year culinary tradition still shows up in the bread, the coffee, and the pasta.
dish1_desc: Pasta tossed with pecorino and black pepper — three ingredients, all about technique.
dish2_desc: Tomato, mozzarella, basil on a charred, chewy crust. The standard everything else gets measured against.
dish3_desc: Espresso-soaked ladyfingers layered with sweet mascarpone — Italy's answer to coffee dessert.

name: Jamaica
cuisine_summary: Jamaican food is bold and fragrant — jerk spice rubbed into meat and cooked over pimento wood smoke, ackee and saltfish at breakfast, and a beef patty culture that gets criminally underestimated everywhere outside the island.
dish1_desc: Chicken marinated in scotch bonnet, allspice, thyme, and ginger, slow-cooked over pimento (allspice) wood. Jamaica's great contribution to global barbecue.
dish2_desc: Ackee fruit (creamy, egg-like when ripe) sautéed with salt cod, onion, tomato, and scotch bonnet. The national dish — eaten at breakfast, sometimes for dinner too.
dish3_desc: Flaky, turmeric-yellow pastry filled with heavily spiced ground beef. The perfect street food — a whole satisfying meal held in one hand.

name: Japan
cuisine_summary: San Francisco's Japantown (Nihonmachi) dates to 1906 and is one of only three remaining historic Japantowns in the United States. At its peak before World War II, it resembled Tokyo's Ginza district. The community rebuilt after the trauma of wartime internment and kept its food culture intact — ramen shops, izakayas, mochi makers, and sushi bars have anchored the Western Addition for decades. Today Japantown draws diners citywide and hosts two Michelin-starred restaurants, making it one of the most culinarily serious Japanese enclaves outside Japan.
dish1_desc: Vinegared rice or pure fish, sliced by someone who's been doing it 20 years. Trust the chef.
dish2_desc: Pork bone broth simmered until milky, with chashu pork, soft egg, and chewy noodles.
dish3_desc: Vegetables and seafood in a crisp, lacy batter. Best straight from the fryer.

name: Jordan
cuisine_summary: Jordanian food is generous and Levantine — mezze spreads with hummus and fattoush, mansaf (the national dish of lamb in fermented yogurt sauce), and a hospitality tradition where no guest leaves hungry.
dish1_desc: Lamb slow-cooked in jameed (fermented dried yogurt) sauce, served over flatbread and saffron rice. Jordan's national dish — the required centerpiece of weddings, funerals, and diplomacy.
dish2_desc: Upside-down rice with chicken or lamb and vegetables, cooked in one pot and ceremonially flipped onto a platter at the table. Dramatic, delicious.
dish3_desc: Crispy toasted flatbread tossed with tomato, cucumber, radish, mint, and a sharp sumac dressing. The Levantine salad that turns stale bread into the best thing on the table.

name: Kazakhstan
cuisine_summary: Kazakh food is nomadic steppe cooking — horse meat and lamb are the proteins, fermented mare's milk is the drink, and the whole tradition is built around hospitality, communal eating, and meat prepared with striking simplicity.
dish1_desc: Boiled lamb or horse meat laid over wide flat noodles and served in broth, eaten by hand. The national dish — the name means 'five fingers.' Cooked for every significant gathering.
dish2_desc: Fried offal (liver, kidney, heart, lung) with onion. A nomadic dish born of practicality — cooked fresh from the parts of a freshly slaughtered animal.
dish3_desc: Fermented mare's milk — slightly fizzy, sour, and mildly alcoholic. The national drink, offered to every guest as a gesture of welcome and respect.

name: Kenya
cuisine_summary: Kenyan food is East African staple cooking with Indian Ocean coastal influences — ugali at every inland meal, nyama choma as the great social occasion, and a Swahili coast where biryani and coconut milk fish tell a different story.
dish1_desc: Goat or beef grilled over charcoal and eaten with your hands. Kenya's great social dish — ordered by weight at a roadside joint, eaten with kachumbari (raw tomato and onion) and ugali.
dish2_desc: Dense white maize porridge — the Kenyan daily staple. Rolled into a ball by hand and used to scoop up meat stew or sukuma wiki. Every meal, every day.
dish3_desc: Collard greens sautéed with onion and tomato. The name means 'push the week' — stretching the budget to Friday. Simple, nutritious, and on every Kenyan table.

name: Korea
cuisine_summary: Korean cuisine is one of the world's most complete — built on fermentation, fire, and communal abundance. Kimchi (fermented vegetables, hundreds of varieties) is not a side dish; it is a pillar of the culture. Banchan — the small plates that fill the table before the main arrives — reflect a philosophy of balance and contrast: cold and hot, sour and savory, crunchy and soft. Tabletop grilling (samgyeopsal, galbi) turns dinner into a social ritual. Sundubu jjigae, doenjang jjigae, and samgyetang are soups with the weight of centuries behind them. Korean food has gone from niche to globally dominant in a single generation — and it earned every bit of the attention.
dish1_desc: Grill cuts like galbi (short rib) and samgyeopsal (pork belly) at your table; wrap in lettuce with rice and ssamjang.
dish2_desc: Rice bowl topped with sautéed vegetables, a fried egg, and gochujang — stir hard before eating.
dish3_desc: Stew of aged kimchi with pork or tuna. Sour, spicy, deeply restorative.

name: Korea (North)
cuisine_summary: North Korean food is cold-noodle culture and mountain cooking — buckwheat noodles in icy broth, kimchi in every variation, and a cuisine closely related to South Korean but shaped by the peninsula's northern geography and colder climate.
dish1_desc: Thin buckwheat noodles served in an icy beef or radish-water broth, topped with sliced cucumber, pear, and a hard-boiled egg. Pyongyang's most famous dish — eaten year-round, not just in summer.
dish2_desc: Fermented cabbage and vegetables seasoned with chile, garlic, and ginger. Present at every North Korean meal — regional styles differ subtly from southern varieties, leaning less spicy.
dish3_desc: Chicken rice soup with egg, scallions, and a clear broth. A Pyongyang specialty — warming, simple, and considered an everyday comfort dish.

name: Kuwait
cuisine_summary: Kuwaiti food is Gulf cooking at its most generous — fragrant rice with dried limes, slow-roasted lamb, fresh shrimp from the Arabian Gulf, and a hospitality culture where the meal never quite ends.
dish1_desc: Spiced rice with lamb, chicken, or shrimp cooked in a fragrant broth with dried limes (loomi) and rose water. Kuwait's essential dish, found at every family table.
dish2_desc: Whole shrimp slow-cooked with rice in a spiced broth. Kuwait's signature seafood rice — a celebration of the Gulf's natural harvest.
dish3_desc: Tender lamb dumplings in a rich, spiced stew. A distinctly Kuwaiti dish — the Gulf's answer to comfort food, eaten in colder months.

name: Kyrgyzstan
cuisine_summary: Kyrgyz food is Central Asian nomadic cooking — lamb and horse meat dominate, dairy is fermented for preservation, and beshbarmak (boiled meat over noodles) anchors every ceremony and celebration.
dish1_desc: Boiled lamb or horse meat served over wide, flat noodles with broth, eaten communally by hand. The national dish — literally 'five fingers.' Cooked for weddings, funerals, and every occasion that matters.
dish2_desc: Hand-pulled noodles in a spiced lamb and vegetable stew. Central Asia's great noodle dish — Chinese in origin, entirely Kyrgyz in character.
dish3_desc: Fermented mare's milk — lightly fizzy, sour, and mildly alcoholic. The traditional nomadic drink, offered to guests and consumed throughout the summer grazing season.

name: Laos
cuisine_summary: Lao food is sticky rice and river fish — freshwater catches, spicy larb salad pounded in a mortar, and padaek (fermented fish paste) that deepens nearly every dish. Gentler than Thai, more herb-forward than Vietnamese.
dish1_desc: Minced meat salad with toasted rice powder, lime juice, fish sauce, shallots, and fresh herbs. Laos's national dish — sharp, fragrant, and eaten at every celebration.
dish2_desc: Glutinous sticky rice steamed in a bamboo basket and eaten by hand, rolled into small balls to scoop up dishes. The Lao staple — present at every single meal.
dish3_desc: Lao-style stew of vegetables, meat, and mai sakaan (a numbing wood spice). Rich, herby, and uniquely Luang Prabang.

name: Latvia
cuisine_summary: Latvian food is Baltic forest and sea — dark rye bread that forms the backbone of every meal, cold-smoked fish, grey peas with bacon, and sour cream on almost everything.
dish1_desc: Grey peas cooked and tossed with crispy fried bacon. Latvia's national dish — simple, ancient, eaten especially at Christmas and Midsummer.
dish2_desc: Rye pastry tart filled with sweetened carrot and potato. A traditional Latvian cake from the Kurzeme region — earthy and gently sweet.
dish3_desc: Cold-smoked Baltic eel laid on buttered dark rye bread. The Latvian coastal delicacy — rich, oily, and perfect with a cold beer.

name: Lebanon
cuisine_summary: Lebanese cuisine is the Middle East's most widely exported and beloved table. The mezze spread is its greatest expression — hummus, baba ganoush, labneh, kibbeh, tabbouleh, fattoush, and warm flatbread arriving in endless rounds. Shawarma, man'oushe (flatbread with za'atar and olive oil), and falafel are street foods that have traveled to every corner of the world. The cuisine is rooted in the Levantine pantry: olive oil, lemon, garlic, fresh herbs, and pomegranate. Lebanese food culture is also inseparable from hospitality — the table is never considered full, and a guest leaving hungry is a genuine failure.
dish1_desc: Smooth chickpea-tahini purée with lemon and good olive oil. Served warm, eaten with bread torn from the pile.
dish2_desc: Marinated meat shaved from a vertical spit, wrapped in flatbread with garlic sauce and pickles.
dish3_desc: Lentils and rice with deeply caramelized onions on top. Humble, perfect, vegetarian.

name: Palestine
cuisine_summary: Palestinian food is Levantine and deeply tied to home cooking — olive oil, sumac, za'atar, slow-cooked rice dishes, and breads wrapped around roasted chicken or vegetables.
dish1_desc: Roasted chicken with sumac, caramelized onions, and olive oil served over taboon bread. The Palestinian table centerpiece.
dish2_desc: Rice, meat, and vegetables cooked in one pot, then flipped upside down onto a platter. Dramatic, fragrant, and built for sharing.
dish3_desc: Shredded pastry layered with cheese or cream, soaked in syrup, and served warm. Nablus is especially famous for it.

name: Lesotho
cuisine_summary: Basotho food is highland Southern African cooking — maize porridge is the bedrock, slow-cooked mutton and offal from the mountain flocks, and wild greens gathered from the Maluti ranges.
dish1_desc: Stiff maize porridge, the Basotho daily staple. Eaten by hand at every meal, used to scoop up relishes, stews, and greens.
dish2_desc: Sheep's or goat's trotters slow-cooked until gelatinous in a spiced stew. A Basotho Sunday and celebration dish.
dish3_desc: Wild leafy greens simmered with onion and tomato. The everyday vegetable side — foraged from the highlands and deeply nutritious.

name: Liberia
cuisine_summary: Liberian food is West African with an American-Liberian twist — palm butter soup is the national dish, cassava and rice are the staples, and the cuisine reflects both indigenous tradition and the freed-slave settlers who founded the country.
dish1_desc: Rich, deep-orange soup made from pounded palm nuts with chicken or fish, dried fish for depth, and hot pepper. Liberia's most beloved dish.
dish2_desc: Pounded cassava or plantain fufu eaten with cassava leaf sauce cooked in palm oil. The everyday staple combination.
dish3_desc: Rice cooked in a tomato and pepper sauce with chicken. The West African constant — Liberian style is slightly sweeter and more heavily spiced.

name: Libya
cuisine_summary: Libyan food is North African with Ottoman and Saharan layers — barley-based dishes, spiced lamb stews, and bazeen (the most distinctively Libyan dish) that tourists rarely encounter but locals swear by.
dish1_desc: Dense, unleavened barley dough formed into a dome and served surrounded by meat stew and hard-boiled eggs. Libya's most traditional dish — eaten by hand from a communal platter.
dish2_desc: Thick wheat or barley porridge eaten sweet with honey and butter, or savory with meat stew. The Libyan comfort food for all occasions.
dish3_desc: Spiced lamb and tomato soup with pasta and a generous hit of harissa. Libya's version of the North African spiced soup — warming and deeply flavored.

name: Lithuania
cuisine_summary: Lithuanian food is Baltic and hearty — cepelinai (potato dumplings the size of small zeppelins), cold pink beet soup in summer, and dark rye bread that underpins every meal.
dish1_desc: Giant boiled potato dumplings stuffed with spiced pork mince, served with sour cream and bacon bits. Lithuania's national dish — filling, substantial, and shaped like a zeppelin.
dish2_desc: Vivid pink cold soup made from kefir, beet, cucumber, hard-boiled egg, and dill. Lithuania's beloved summer dish — refreshing and unlike anything else.
dish3_desc: Karaite-origin pastry filled with lamb or pork and onion. A specialty of Trakai — flaky, juicy, and tied to Lithuania's Crimean Karaite minority.

name: Luxembourg
cuisine_summary: Luxembourgish food is small-country cooking at its most satisfying — German heartiness, French finesse, and Belgian influences all meeting over smoked pork and beans, and a pastry culture that punches above its size.
dish1_desc: Smoked pork collar served with broad beans in a cream sauce. Luxembourg's national dish — rich, smoky, and the thing every Luxembourger grows up eating.
dish2_desc: Crispy potato fritters with onion and parsley, sold at Luxembourg's Schueberfouer fair. The national street snack.
dish3_desc: Veal and pork pâté baked in a pastry shell with a Riesling jelly interior. A Luxembourgish specialty served at celebrations.

name: Madagascar
cuisine_summary: Malagasy food is rice three times a day without apology — zebu beef stew, coconut milk, and a cuisine shaped by the island's Austronesian, African, and Arab roots. Vary (rice) is not a side dish; it is the meal.
dish1_desc: Zebu beef braised with fresh ginger and a mix of leafy greens (brèdes). Madagascar's national dish — light, fragrant, and always served over rice.
dish2_desc: Pounded cassava leaves slow-cooked with pork and coconut milk. Rich, dark green, and deeply satisfying — the country's most comforting stew.
dish3_desc: Rice cooked with leafy greens and a little meat or fish. The everyday Malagasy staple — simple, nutritious, eaten morning and night.

name: Malawi
cuisine_summary: Malawian food is Lake Malawi and maize — nsima porridge at every meal, chambo (a prized freshwater fish) grilled over charcoal, and relishes of beans and green vegetables that make the staple come alive.
dish1_desc: Stiff white maize porridge rolled into balls and eaten by hand. The Malawian daily staple — present at every meal, every day, for most of the population.
dish2_desc: Freshwater cichlid from Lake Malawi, grilled whole over charcoal or fried. Malawi's prized fish — flaky, mild, and the centerpiece of any celebration meal.
dish3_desc: Relish of beans, vegetables, or meat eaten alongside nsima. The concept is as important as any single recipe — ndiwo means 'the thing that goes with nsima.'

name: Malaysia
cuisine_summary: Malaysian food is a Southeast Asian crossroads — Malay, Chinese, and Indian flavors coexisting on every street and in every hawker center. No cuisine in the world packs this much variety into this small a space.
dish1_desc: Coconut-scented rice with sambal, crispy anchovies, roasted peanuts, cucumber, and a boiled egg. Malaysia's national dish — eaten for breakfast, lunch, and dinner without apology.
dish2_desc: Flat rice noodles stir-fried over fierce heat with Chinese sausage, shrimp, egg, and bean sprouts in dark soy. The wok hei (breath of the wok) is everything.
dish3_desc: Coconut milk noodle soup with shrimp, fish cake, and cockles. The Peranakan classic — every town has a version, every version has partisans.

name: Maldives
cuisine_summary: Maldivian food is tuna and coconut in every combination — the island nation's two great resources. Smoked skipjack tuna (mas) appears at breakfast, in soups, and as a snack. Everything else supports these two ingredients.
dish1_desc: Shredded smoked tuna mixed with coconut, onion, chili, and lime. Eaten for breakfast with roshi flatbread. The Maldivian morning ritual.
dish2_desc: Clear, delicate broth of skipjack tuna simmered with salt. The national soup — profound in its simplicity, eaten with rice, lime, and chili paste.
dish3_desc: Samosa-like pastry filled with smoked tuna, hard-boiled egg, and onion. A Maldivian street snack with South Asian influence.

name: Mali
cuisine_summary: Malian food is Sahelian grain cooking — millet and rice form the base, tigadegena (peanut stew) is the national sauce, and the cuisine flows along the Niger River from Timbuktu to Bamako.
dish1_desc: Peanut butter stew with beef or chicken, tomatoes, and sweet potato. Mali's most beloved sauce — rich, thick, and eaten over rice or tô.
dish2_desc: Stiff millet or sorghum paste eaten by hand and dipped into peanut or leaf sauces. The Malian daily staple for the majority of the population.
dish3_desc: Rice cooked slowly in a tomato, onion, and meat broth until each grain is deeply flavored. The festive dish — served at weddings and naming ceremonies.

name: Malta
