cuisine_summary: Maltese food is Mediterranean island cooking shaped by centuries of Arab, Sicilian, and British occupation — rabbit is the national meat, pastizzi are the national snack, and the cuisine is more layered than the island's small size suggests.
dish1_desc: Rabbit marinated in wine and garlic, fried then braised slowly until tender. Malta's national dish — eaten on Sundays, at restaurants, and at every family gathering.
dish2_desc: Flaky diamond-shaped pastry filled with ricotta or mushy peas. Malta's beloved street snack — sold at pastizzerias from dawn, eaten at every hour.
dish3_desc: Thin beef slices stuffed with a filling of breadcrumbs, bacon, and egg, rolled and braised in wine. The Maltese beef olive — a slow Sunday dish.

name: Mauritania
cuisine_summary: Mauritanian food is Saharan and Sahelian — camel milk, rice cooked in fish broth, and a nomadic tradition of slow-roasted lamb. The cuisine sits at the crossroads of North African and West African cooking.
dish1_desc: Rice cooked in a rich tomato-and-fish broth with vegetables. Shared with Senegal but deeply embedded in Mauritanian culture — the most important daily dish.
dish2_desc: Whole lamb slow-roasted over charcoal until the skin is crackling-crisp. The Saharan celebration feast — made for weddings and Eid.
dish3_desc: Camel milk thinned with water and lightly sweetened. The traditional Mauritanian drink — refreshing in the desert heat, offered to every guest.

name: Mauritius
cuisine_summary: Mauritian food is one of the Indian Ocean's great multicultural cuisines — Indian, African, Chinese, and French traditions stirred together over centuries, producing dishes that belong to no single heritage and to all of them.
dish1_desc: Thin flatbread filled with ground yellow split peas, served with a variety of curries and chutneys. The Mauritian street food — eaten standing at a roadside stall.
dish2_desc: Spiced tomato sauce with fish, sausage, or prawns, eaten over rice. The everyday Mauritian dish — French Creole in origin and universally loved.
dish3_desc: Deep-fried split pea fritters spiked with chili and turmeric. The Port Louis street snack — eaten in the morning with a cup of tea.

name: Mexico
cuisine_summary: Mexican food is woven into San Francisco's DNA. The Mission District has been a Latino heartland since the 1950s, and it gave the world one of its most iconic food inventions: the Mission-style burrito, born at Taquería La Cumbre in 1967. La Palma Mexicatessen has been pressing fresh masa by hand on 24th Street since 1953. Today the Mission is lined with taquerías, panaderías, and restaurants serving regional Mexican cuisine from Oaxaca, Jalisco, and beyond — a living neighborhood built on tortillas, mole, and generations of immigrant labor.
dish1_desc: Slow-cooked pork shoulder, crisped and piled into corn tortillas with onion and cilantro.
dish2_desc: Hominy stew with pork in a chile broth — garnish-your-own with cabbage, radish, lime.
dish3_desc: Roasted poblano peppers stuffed with cheese, dipped in egg batter, and fried golden.

name: Moldova
cuisine_summary: Moldovan food is Eastern European peasant cooking with a wine-country warmth — mamaliga (golden cornmeal porridge), stuffed cabbage rolls, and a sour soup culture that reflects both Romanian and Ukrainian neighbors.
dish1_desc: Thick yellow cornmeal porridge, cooked to a smooth solidity. Moldova's ancient staple — eaten with bryndza sheep's cheese, sour cream, or alongside meat stew.
dish2_desc: Pork and rice stuffed into cabbage leaves and braised in tomato sauce with thyme. The Moldovan national comfort dish — slow, rich, and made for winter.
dish3_desc: Chicken noodle soup with lemon juice, lovage, and sour cream. Moldova's restorative everyday soup — tangy, warming, and deeply homey.

name: Mongolia
cuisine_summary: Mongolian food is nomadic and meat-and-dairy at its most essential — boiled mutton, fermented mare's milk, and hand-made dumplings. The open steppe shapes everything: few vegetables, maximum protein, cooked simply over fire.
dish1_desc: Steamed dumplings filled with spiced minced mutton or beef. Mongolia's national dish — made by the hundred for Tsagaan Sar (Lunar New Year) and eaten year-round.
dish2_desc: Homemade noodles stir-fried with mutton and whatever vegetables are available. The Mongolian everyday noodle dish — filling and adaptable.
dish3_desc: Fermented mare's milk — lightly fizzy, sour, and mildly alcoholic. The ancient nomadic drink central to Mongolian hospitality and summer culture.

name: Montenegro
cuisine_summary: Montenegrin food straddles the Adriatic coast and the Balkan interior — smoked mountain ham, grilled seafood, and a cuisine that shares genes with Serbia but has its own mountain character shaped by the Dinaric Alps.
dish1_desc: Air-dried smoked ham from the Njeguši village on Mount Lovćen. Montenegro's most prized product — dense, smoky, sliced paper-thin and eaten with local cheese.
dish2_desc: Cornmeal and potato porridge enriched with kajmak (clotted cream) and local cheese. Mountain comfort food — heavy, warming, made for cold Dinaric winters.
dish3_desc: Black squid ink risotto from the Adriatic coast towns. Rich and dramatic — the sea's umami in every grain of rice.

name: Morocco
cuisine_summary: Moroccan food is North Africa's most complex and celebrated — spice blends (ras el hanout, chermoula) that took generations to perfect, slow tagines in conical clay vessels, and a couscous culture that is UNESCO-protected.
dish1_desc: Slow-cooked stew of lamb, chicken, or fish with preserved lemon, olives, and spices, cooked in a conical clay vessel that concentrates the steam. The Moroccan method — patient, fragrant, irreplaceable.
dish2_desc: Flaky warqa pastry filled with spiced pigeon (or chicken) and almonds, dusted with cinnamon and powdered sugar. A Fez showpiece — savory and sweet at once.
dish3_desc: Thick tomato and chickpea soup with lamb, lentils, and fresh herbs. The soup that breaks the Ramadan fast each sunset — warming, spiced, and deeply nourishing.

name: Mozambique
cuisine_summary: Mozambican food is Portuguese colonial legacy meeting East African ingredients — piri piri heat, giant Indian Ocean prawns, and coconut milk in almost everything. The food of the coast is some of the best seafood cooking in Africa.
dish1_desc: Giant tiger prawns marinated in piri piri sauce and grilled over charcoal. Mozambique's greatest dish — Maputo's signature plate, eaten on the seafront.
dish2_desc: Cassava leaf stew cooked in coconut milk with ground peanuts and shrimp. A traditional dish of the coast — complex, green, and deeply satisfying.
dish3_desc: Smooth white maize porridge. The Mozambican daily staple — eaten alongside every fish, meat, or vegetable dish.

name: Namibia
cuisine_summary: Namibian food is game meat, biltong, and potjiekos from the Southern African tradition — oryx, kudu, and springbok alongside Oshiwambo staples of maize porridge and mopane worms from the north.
dish1_desc: Freshly grilled beef sold at open-air markets, seasoned with spices and sliced to order. Windhoek's great street food — eaten standing, the social ritual of the city.
dish2_desc: Stiff maize or pearl millet porridge — the staple of northern Namibia's Oshiwambo people. Eaten by hand with meat stew or spinach relish.
dish3_desc: Air-dried, spiced game meat (kudu, oryx, or beef). Southern Africa's great preservation tradition — chewy, intensely savory, and eaten as a snack throughout the day.

name: Nepal
cuisine_summary: Nepali food is dal bhat twice a day without question — lentil soup over rice with vegetable sides. Momos (dumplings) are the beloved snack from Kathmandu street corners, and the cuisine shifts from Indian plains to Tibetan highlands as you climb.
dish1_desc: Lentil soup poured over steamed rice with vegetable sides (tarkari) and pickle (achar). Eaten twice daily by most Nepalis. 'Dal bhat power, 24 hour' is not a slogan — it is a fact.
dish2_desc: Steamed or pan-fried dumplings filled with spiced buffalo meat or vegetables, served with a fiery tomato-sesame dipping sauce. Nepal's beloved snack — sold at every street corner in Kathmandu.
dish3_desc: Tibetan-influenced noodle soup with vegetables or meat in a warming spiced broth. The high-altitude comfort dish — popular across the Himalayan region.

name: Netherlands
cuisine_summary: Dutch food is quieter than its neighbors but deeply satisfying — raw herring eaten at street stalls, stamppot in winter, aged Gouda that crystallizes on your tongue, and stroopwafels balanced on a hot mug to soften the caramel.
dish1_desc: Raw salt-cured herring eaten whole at a street stall — held by the tail, tilted back, with raw onion and pickle. The Dutch street food ritual, consumed mostly in May when the new season arrives.
dish2_desc: Mashed potato combined with kale, sauerkraut, or endive, served with a smoked sausage (rookworst). The Dutch winter dish — warming, starchy, and entirely unpretentious.
dish3_desc: Two thin crispy waffle discs sandwiched with a sticky caramel-syrup filling. Best balanced on top of a hot mug until the caramel softens. The Dutch office essential.

name: New Zealand
cuisine_summary: New Zealand food is Pacific and multicultural — Māori hāngī earth-oven tradition, world-class lamb and dairy, and an increasingly confident modern cuisine that uses native ingredients like horopito and kawakawa.
dish1_desc: Meat and vegetables slow-cooked in an underground earth oven on heated volcanic stones, wrapped in foil or leaves. The Māori feast tradition — smoky, tender, and deeply communal.
dish2_desc: Crisp meringue shell with a soft marshmallow interior, topped with whipped cream and kiwifruit. New Zealand and Australia both claim it. New Zealand is correct.
dish3_desc: New Zealand lamb roasted simply with herbs and garlic. Some of the world's most flavorful lamb, raised on lush green pasture — the Sunday centerpiece.

name: Nicaragua
cuisine_summary: Nicaraguan food is Central American home cooking — gallo pinto made with red beans (not black), vigorón served on banana leaves, and nacatamales on Sunday mornings. Unpretentious, filling, and deeply tied to family tradition.
dish1_desc: Red kidney beans and rice cooked together and seasoned with Worcestershire and onion. Nicaragua's national breakfast — different from Costa Rica's version in bean color and flavor, and Nicaraguans will make sure you know it.
dish2_desc: Boiled yuca topped with chicharrón (pork crackling) and a tangy pickled cabbage slaw, served on a banana leaf. Granada's famous street food — textures and flavors in every bite.
dish3_desc: Large corn masa tamale filled with pork, potato, rice, tomato, and mint, wrapped in banana leaves and steamed. The Nicaraguan Sunday morning tradition — made the night before, eaten slowly.

name: Niger
cuisine_summary: Nigerien food is Sahelian grain cooking shaped by the Sahara's edge — millet porridge (tô or dambou), dried and spiced meat (kilishi), and the Hausa and Tuareg traditions that define the country's culinary identity.
dish1_desc: Millet couscous steamed and served with a vegetable and meat sauce. Niger's everyday staple — filling, simple, and eaten across the country.
dish2_desc: Thin strips of beef or goat marinated in a spiced peanut paste and sun-dried until chewy. The Hausa equivalent of biltong — intensely flavored and sold at every market.
dish3_desc: Millet balls (fura) crushed and mixed with chilled fermented cow's milk (nono). The traditional Fulani nomad's sustenance — drunk as a thick beverage across the Sahel.

name: Nigeria
cuisine_summary: Nigerian food is West Africa's most populous and loudest culinary voice — jollof rice that wins every Twitter argument, egusi soup eaten with pounded yam, and suya skewers at midnight roadside stalls. The food is bold, and so is everything about it.
dish1_desc: Rice cooked in a smoky, spiced tomato-and-pepper base until each grain is stained red and deeply flavored. Nigeria defends this dish with extraordinary passion. The party jollof — cooked outdoors over wood fire — is in a class of its own.
dish2_desc: Ground melon seeds cooked with palm oil, stockfish, leafy greens, and assorted meat. Eaten with pounded yam or fufu — rich, textured, and the backbone of Nigerian cooking.
dish3_desc: Thin-sliced beef or chicken coated in a spiced peanut (yaji) rub and grilled over charcoal. Nigeria's great street food — served on newspaper with raw onion and tomato at midnight.

name: North Macedonia
cuisine_summary: Macedonian food is Balkan peasant cooking with Ottoman pastry layers — grilled meats over charcoal, a national baked bean dish in a clay pot, and ajvar (roasted pepper relish) that every household makes in autumn.
dish1_desc: White beans baked with peppers, onion, and tomato in a clay pot until thick and caramelized. North Macedonia's national dish — simple, earthy, and deeply satisfying.
dish2_desc: Roasted red pepper and eggplant relish made every autumn in enormous batches. Eaten with white bread and sheep's cheese through winter — Macedonia's essential condiment.
dish3_desc: Oval flatbread covered with marinated pork chunks and a cracked egg, baked until the edges crisp. The Macedonian pizza — and the reason to visit Štip.

name: Norway
cuisine_summary: Norwegian food is Arctic and coastal — cured salmon, wind-dried cod, lamb and cabbage stew, and a brown cheese that tastes like caramel and confuses every visitor until it doesn't. The new Nordic wave started here too.
dish1_desc: Salmon cured with salt, sugar, and dill for 48 hours, sliced paper-thin and served with mustard-dill sauce on rye crispbread. Norway's most elegant dish — ancient and simple.
dish2_desc: Lamb and whole cabbage cooked together with black pepper in a large pot until collapsing. Norway's national dish — declared by vote, celebrated every autumn.
dish3_desc: Brown whey cheese with a sweet, fudgy caramel flavor. Shaved onto crispbread at every Norwegian breakfast — an acquired taste that Norwegians consider non-negotiable.

name: Oman
cuisine_summary: Omani food is ancient Arabian Peninsula cooking fragrant with frankincense-trade spices — shuwa (underground pit-roasted lamb) is the great ceremonial dish, dried limes perfume the rice, and halwa sweets are served with coffee to every guest.
dish1_desc: Spiced lamb or goat wrapped in banana leaves and slow-roasted in an underground sand oven for up to 48 hours. Oman's great ceremonial dish — made for Eid and weddings, impossibly tender.
dish2_desc: Fragrant spiced rice with fish, chicken, or lamb cooked with dried limes (loomi) and rose water. Oman's essential everyday rice dish.
dish3_desc: Soft, gelatinous sweet made from sugar, ghee, rosewater, and saffron, studded with nuts. Served in small bowls with cardamom coffee to every guest — the taste of Omani hospitality.

name: Pakistan
cuisine_summary: Pakistani food is South Asia's most meat-forward and spice-bold — slow-simmered nihari for breakfast, karahi cooked fast in a heavy wok, and a biryani tradition in Karachi that is richer and more intensely spiced than anywhere else.
dish1_desc: Slow-cooked beef shank stew with whole spices and bone marrow, simmered overnight and eaten at breakfast. Lahore and Karachi's great morning dish — served with naan and a squeeze of lemon.
dish2_desc: Chicken or lamb cooked fast in a heavy iron wok with tomatoes, fresh ginger, and green chiles. The quintessential Pakistani restaurant dish — smoky, direct, and deeply satisfying.
dish3_desc: Fragrant basmati rice layered with spiced meat and potatoes, richer and more intensely flavored than Indian varieties. Karachi's biryani is a source of municipal pride.

name: Panama
cuisine_summary: Panamanian food is a Central American crossroads — sancocho stew is the national dish, seafood arrives from two oceans (Pacific and Caribbean), and a diverse population has left Chinese, West Indian, and Indigenous fingerprints on the cuisine.
dish1_desc: Chicken and root vegetable stew with culantro (the wild herb), ñame, and corn on the cob. Panama's national dish — eaten on weekends, at celebrations, and as a cure for everything.
dish2_desc: Fish or shrimp cured in lime juice with ají chombo chile and onion. Served cold with crackers — Panama's take on the Pacific ceviche tradition.
dish3_desc: Shredded beef braised in tomato sauce with peppers and onion, served over white rice. The everyday Panamanian comfort plate.

name: Papua New Guinea
cuisine_summary: Papua New Guinean food is one of the world's most diverse — over 800 languages and 800 food cultures, united by earth-oven cooking, root vegetables, and coconut. The mumu feast is the great communal tradition.
dish1_desc: Pork, sweet potato, cassava, and greens slow-cooked together in an earth oven on heated stones, wrapped in banana leaves. Papua New Guinea's great communal feast — smoky, tender, and deeply shared.
dish2_desc: Sago palm starch formed into dumplings or porridge. The staple of coastal and lowland PNG — starchy, neutral, eaten with fish or coconut sauce.
dish3_desc: Sweet potato roasted directly in embers or baked in the earth oven. The everyday staple of the Highlands — simple, naturally sweet, and deeply relied upon.

name: Paraguay
cuisine_summary: Paraguayan food is South America's most overlooked — cassava replaces potato in nearly everything, sopa paraguaya (despite the name) is a baked corn bread, and the cuisine is built around the asado and the chipa cheese bread.
dish1_desc: Despite meaning 'Paraguayan soup,' this is a dense savory corn and cheese bake. Rich, filling, and eaten alongside grilled meat — the national side dish.
dish2_desc: Cheese and cassava flour bread rings baked in a tatakua (clay oven). Paraguay's beloved snack — sold on every bus, at every roadside, warm and stretchy.
dish3_desc: Beef ribs and cuts slow-grilled over wood coals. Paraguay's version of the Southern Cone asado — unhurried, smoky, the centerpiece of every weekend.

name: Peru
cuisine_summary: Peruvian cuisine is arguably the most exciting in the world right now — and it has been building toward this moment for centuries. Ceviche, cured in tiger's milk (lime, chile, and fish juices), is the national icon: bright, acidic, and consumed at cevicherías by the millions. Lomo saltado merges Chinese stir-fry technique with Andean beef and potatoes — a legacy of the 19th-century Chinese immigrant community (the Chifa tradition). Causa, anticuchos, ají de gallina, and the 3,000 varieties of native potato tell a story of Indigenous Andean cuisine that fed civilizations before the Spanish arrived. Lima is now home to multiple restaurants on the World's 50 Best list, led by Central, Maido, and Astrid y Gastón. Peru didn't just find its culinary voice — it became one of the loudest on the planet.
dish1_desc: Beef stir-fried with onions, tomato, and soy sauce — served over rice with fries. The Peru-China crossover hit.
dish2_desc: Raw white fish cured in lime, chile, and red onion. Cold, bright, addictive.
dish3_desc: Shredded chicken in a creamy aji amarillo sauce, served over rice and potato.

name: Philippines
cuisine_summary: SoMa Pilipinas — officially recognized as SF's Filipino Cultural Heritage District in 2016 — honors over 120 years of Filipino presence in the city. Filipino merchant marines put down roots at South Park in 1921, and the community has been in SoMa ever since. For most of that time, Filipino food was SF's best-kept secret — adobo, kare-kare, and lechon fed the community quietly while the rest of the city looked elsewhere. That's changing fast: a new generation of Filipino chefs is bringing lumpia, sisig, and ube to the mainstream, making SoMa one of the city's most exciting food destinations.
dish1_desc: Chicken or pork braised in vinegar, soy, garlic, and bay. Every family has their version.
dish2_desc: Sizzling chopped pork (jowl + ear, classically) with onion, chile, and citrus. Eat with rice and a cold beer.
dish3_desc: Shaved ice with sweet beans, jellies, fruit, ube ice cream, and evaporated milk. Stir before eating.

name: Poland
cuisine_summary: Polish food is Eastern European peasant cooking elevated by centuries of refinement — pierogi stuffed with everything imaginable, beet soup with tiny dumplings, and bigos (hunter's stew) that improves every time you reheat it.
dish1_desc: Boiled or pan-fried dumplings stuffed with potato and cheese, sauerkraut and mushroom, or meat. Poland's most beloved dish — made in large batches, eaten with sour cream and fried onion.
dish2_desc: Sauerkraut and fresh cabbage stew with mixed pork, sausage, mushrooms, and sometimes prunes. The hunter's stew — better the second day, best the third.
dish3_desc: Sour fermented rye soup with hard-boiled egg and white kielbasa, often served inside a bread bowl. Poland's most distinctive and proudly national soup.

name: Portugal
cuisine_summary: Portuguese food is ocean-facing and unhurried — salt cod prepared in a different way every day of the year, piri piri chicken, and custard tarts from Belém that set the global standard for what a pastry can be.
dish1_desc: Salt cod shredded and scrambled with thin-cut fried potato and egg, finished with olives and parsley. One of the 365 ways to cook bacalhau — and one of the best.
dish2_desc: Flaky custard tarts from Belém, baked at high heat until blistered and caramelized. Eaten warm with cinnamon — the most perfect thing Portugal has given the world.
dish3_desc: Potato and dark kale soup with a slice of chouriço. The national soup — simple, green, essential, and found at every Portuguese table from north to south.

name: Qatar
cuisine_summary: Qatari food is Gulf cooking with a generous hand — machboos rice is the centerpiece, slow-cooked lamb appears at every celebration, and the tradition of hospitality means coffee and dates arrive before any question is asked.
dish1_desc: Spiced basmati rice cooked with lamb, chicken, or shrimp in a fragrant broth with loomi (dried limes) and rose water. Qatar's national dish — the Gulf rice that defines the cuisine.
dish2_desc: Slow-cooked wheat and lamb beaten together until smooth and porridge-like. The Ramadan staple — silky, ancient, deeply satisfying in its simplicity.
dish3_desc: Sweet vermicelli noodles perfumed with saffron, cardamom, and rose water, topped with a savory omelet. Qatar's surprising and distinctively Qatari breakfast.

name: Romania
cuisine_summary: Romanian food is Balkan and Eastern European — golden polenta, sour soups that use fermented bran for tartness, grilled skinless sausages, and slow-braised stews that have been cooking since the Ottoman era.
dish1_desc: Yellow cornmeal porridge cooked to a firm consistency, Romania's ancient staple. Eaten with bryndza cheese, sour cream, and fried egg — sometimes as the entire meal.
dish2_desc: Skinless grilled sausages made from a blend of beef, pork, and lamb with garlic and caraway. Romania's great street and barbecue food — eaten with mustard at every outdoor gathering.
dish3_desc: Sour tripe soup enriched with sour cream, garlic, and vinegar. Romania's famous hangover remedy — tart, rich, and deeply restorative.

name: Russia
cuisine_summary: Russian cuisine is as vast and climatically extreme as the country itself — a tradition built on survival, preservation, and unexpected elegance. Borscht (beet and cabbage soup) warms millions from Moscow to Vladivostok. Pelmeni — Siberian meat dumplings eaten with sour cream — are the cold-weather comfort food of an entire civilization. Blini with caviar and smoked fish represent the aristocratic table; black bread and pickled vegetables represent the peasant one. The pickling, fermenting, and curing traditions — born of necessity through brutal winters — produced some of the world's most complex preserved foods. Vodka is less a drink than a social institution.
dish1_desc: Deep red beet and beef soup with cabbage, carrot, and potato, served with a generous spoonful of sour cream and black bread on the side. Russia's most iconic soup.
dish2_desc: Small meat dumplings boiled and served with sour cream or butter and dill. Siberia's great contribution — made in batches of hundreds and frozen for winter use.
dish3_desc: Beef strips in a sour cream and mushroom sauce, served over egg noodles. A 19th-century St. Petersburg dish that became a global classic.

name: Rwanda
cuisine_summary: Rwandan food is East African staple cooking — beans are the cornerstone protein, ugali and sweet potato are the starches, and brochettes (grilled skewers) are the social street food of Kigali's evenings.
dish1_desc: Pounded cassava leaves cooked with eggplant and palm oil. The most common everyday dish in Rwanda — earthy, rich, and deeply nourishing.
dish2_desc: Goat or beef skewers grilled over charcoal at street stalls throughout Kigali. Rwanda's great social food — eaten with friends, cold beer optional but recommended.
dish3_desc: Mashed sweet potatoes seasoned simply with butter and salt. A beloved Rwandan side dish — naturally sweet and satisfying.

name: Saint Lucia
cuisine_summary: Saint Lucian food is Caribbean Creole with a French accent — green fig (unripe banana) and salt fish is the national dish, and everything from the coast arrives in coconut milk or with a hit of Scotch bonnet pepper.
dish1_desc: Boiled unripe banana with salt cod sautéed in onion, tomato, and peppers. Saint Lucia's national dish — the 'fig' is banana; the combination is perfect.
dish2_desc: Dasheen leaf soup blended with coconut milk, okra, crab, and spices. The Caribbean island staple — deeply green, rich, and nourishing.
dish3_desc: Salt cod fritters — light, crispy, and eaten as a street snack across the Eastern Caribbean. The Lucian version is spiced with scotch bonnet and herbs.

name: Saudi Arabia
cuisine_summary: Saudi food is Gulf and Hejazi — kabsa (the national rice dish with dried limes and whole spices) is eaten communally from a vast platter, whole-roasted lamb appears at every celebration, and dates and coffee frame every social encounter.
dish1_desc: Basmati rice cooked with lamb, chicken, or camel in a spiced broth with black lime, cardamom, and cinnamon. Saudi Arabia's national dish — eaten from a communal platter, always with one hand.
dish2_desc: Whole lamb slow-roasted in a tandoor-like underground clay oven over rice until impossibly tender. The Arabian Peninsula's celebration feast — fragrant, smoky, and magnificent.
dish3_desc: Crushed wheat cooked with chicken or lamb broth until smooth and porridge-like, spiced with cumin and cinnamon. One of Saudi Arabia's oldest dishes — pre-Islamic in origin.

name: Senegal
cuisine_summary: Senegalese food is West Africa's most celebrated cuisine — thiéboudienne is the original jollof rice, yassa is the chicken dish the whole region loves, and the cooking is built on a hospitality tradition (teranga) where feeding guests is a moral obligation.
dish1_desc: Rice cooked in a spiced tomato-and-fish broth with stuffed fish and vegetables. The origin of jollof rice — Senegal's national dish and its proudest culinary claim. 'Thiébou' means rice, 'dienne' means fish.
dish2_desc: Chicken marinated overnight in lemon juice and mustard, braised with mountains of caramelized onions until deeply fragrant. Tangy, sweet, and one of West Africa's most beloved dishes.
dish3_desc: Beef or lamb slow-cooked in a rich, thick peanut butter sauce with sweet potato and tomato. Senegal's other great dish — dark, dense, and eaten over rice.

name: Serbia
cuisine_summary: Serbian food is Balkan roštilj (grill) culture and Ottoman pastry legacy — grilled minced meat sausages, stuffed sauerkraut rolls, and slow bean soups. Rakija plum brandy accompanies everything.
dish1_desc: Skinless minced beef and pork sausages grilled over charcoal, served with raw onion, kajmak clotted cream, and ajvar relish. Serbia's essential barbecue and street food.
dish2_desc: Sauerkraut cabbage leaves stuffed with pork and rice, slow-braised in tomato broth. The Serbian winter Sunday dish — made in large quantities, improving every day.
dish3_desc: White bean soup cooked with smoked pork and sweet paprika until thick and silky. The Serbian peasant dish — slow, earthy, and deeply satisfying.

name: Seychelles
cuisine_summary: Seychellois cuisine is Indian Ocean Creole at its most layered — a product of French colonialism, African roots, Indian spice traditions, and Chinese influence, all stirred together on a remote archipelago of 115 islands. Fresh reef fish — red snapper, grouper, tuna — is the cornerstone, cooked in coconut milk curries fragrant with lemongrass and turmeric. Shark chutney (smoked shark mixed with bilimbi fruit and turmeric) is the most distinctively Seychellois dish. The spice garden of the islands produces cinnamon, vanilla, and cloves that perfume both the food and the air.
dish1_desc: Fresh catch (red snapper or grouper) marinated in Creole spices — ginger, turmeric, chili, garlic — and grilled over coals. The daily island staple.
dish2_desc: Ripe banana or breadfruit cooked in sweetened coconut milk with vanilla and nutmeg. A Seychellois dessert or sweet side dish — tropical and comforting.
dish3_desc: Smoked shark blended with bilimbi (sour fruit) and spices into a pungent condiment. A uniquely Seychellois preparation eaten with rice and curry.

name: Sierra Leone
cuisine_summary: Sierra Leonean food is West African with a Krio (Creole) accent — cassava leaf stew is the national dish, groundnut stew is the everyday comfort, and the cuisine reflects the history of freed slaves returning from the Americas.
dish1_desc: Pounded cassava leaves slow-cooked with palm oil, dried fish, smoked fish, and beef or chicken. Sierra Leone's national dish — deeply umami, rich, and unlike anything else.
dish2_desc: Rich peanut stew with chicken, tomatoes, and chili. The universal West African comfort dish — thick enough to stand a spoon in, eaten over rice.
dish3_desc: Rice cooked in a spiced tomato and fish sauce. Sierra Leone's version leans heavily on dried and smoked fish for depth — intensely flavored and distinctive.

name: Singapore
cuisine_summary: Singaporean food is the world's greatest hawker center culture — Hainanese chicken rice, Peranakan laksa, and chili crab exist alongside hundreds of stalls serving Chinese, Malay, and Indian dishes. The queues are always worth it.
dish1_desc: Poached chicken served over rice cooked in chicken stock and fat, with ginger-scallion sauce, dark soy, and chili sauce. Singapore's national dish — judged by the quality of the rice as much as the chicken.
dish2_desc: Coconut milk noodle soup with shrimp, fishcake, cockles, and a complex spice paste. The Peranakan classic — each neighborhood has a version it defends.
dish3_desc: Whole mud crab stir-fried in a thick, semi-sweet, spiced tomato-and-chili sauce. Singapore's most famous seafood dish — eaten with fried mantou buns to mop up every drop of sauce.

name: Slovakia
cuisine_summary: Slovak food is Central European mountain cooking — bryndzové halušky (the national dish of potato dumplings with sheep cheese) defines the cuisine, along with sauerkraut soups, pork preparations, and potato flatbreads.
dish1_desc: Small, soft potato dumplings tossed with creamy bryndza (Slovak sheep's cheese) and topped with crispy fried bacon. Slovakia's national dish — rich, uniquely flavored, and not like anything else in Central Europe.
dish2_desc: Sauerkraut soup with smoked sausage, mushrooms, and sour cream. The Slovak Christmas Eve tradition — served as the first meal after fasting.
dish3_desc: Thin potato flatbreads cooked on a dry griddle, eaten with goose fat or rolled around a poppy seed and plum jam filling. The Slovak snack and side dish.

name: Slovenia
cuisine_summary: Slovenian food sits at the crossroads of Alpine, Adriatic, and Pannonian cooking — štruklji (rolled dumplings) in every filling imaginable, pumpkin seed oil drizzled over everything, and potica (rolled nut cake) at every celebration.
dish1_desc: Rolled dumplings made from pasta or filo dough and filled with cottage cheese, walnut, or tarragon. Slovenia's most distinctive dish — boiled or baked, sweet or savory.
dish2_desc: A rolled cake with walnut, poppy seed, or tarragon filling inside a yeasted dough. The Slovenian celebration pastry — essential at Easter and Christmas, judged by how many layers it has.
dish3_desc: Sauerkraut and bean soup with pork ribs, slow-cooked until thick and deeply flavored. The traditional dish of the Karst region — hearty, sour, and warming.

name: Somalia
cuisine_summary: Somali food is aromatic and distinctive — canjeero (spongy flatbread) is the staple, bariis iskukaris is the spiced rice of celebrations, and the cuisine carries Indian Ocean trade route spices (cumin, cardamom, cloves) in everything.
dish1_desc: Spiced basmati rice cooked with raisins, onion, and whole spices — cumin, cardamom, cloves. Somalia's aromatic celebration rice — served at weddings and Eid.
dish2_desc: Soft, spongy fermented flatbread made from sorghum or corn flour. The Somali daily staple — eaten with honey and butter at breakfast or alongside savory stews.
dish3_desc: Diced beef or camel quickly stir-fried with cumin, onion, and banana pepper. A fast, flavorful everyday meat dish — served over rice or with canjeero.

name: South Africa
cuisine_summary: South African food is braai smoke and Cape Malay spice — boerewors sausage over wood fire, bobotie (the national dish) with its Cape Malay roots, and bunny chow (curry in a hollowed bread loaf) from Durban's Indian community.
dish1_desc: Southern African barbecue: boerewors (coiled beef-and-pork sausage), lamb chops, and steak cooked over wood fire. The South African social institution — more ritual than recipe, attended by all.
dish2_desc: Spiced minced beef with a savory egg custard topping, baked until golden. Cape Malay in origin, now South Africa's national dish — sweet, fragrant, and unlike any other.
dish3_desc: Half a hollowed-out white loaf filled with lamb, chicken, or bean curry. Durban's great contribution to world food — Indian immigrant origin, universally eaten.

name: South Sudan
cuisine_summary: South Sudanese food is East African staple cooking shaped by the Nile — asida (sorghum porridge) is the daily foundation, slow-stewed meats and greens are the relishes, and the cuisine reflects the country's Nilotic and Equatorian peoples.
dish1_desc: Thick sorghum or maize porridge, the South Sudanese daily staple. Eaten by hand from a communal bowl, used to scoop up meat stew or green vegetable sauce.
dish2_desc: Slow-cooked fava beans mashed with oil and spices. Shared across the Nile Valley — eaten for breakfast throughout South Sudan.
dish3_desc: Goat braised low and slow with tomato, onion, and dried chili. The celebration meat dish — present at every significant gathering.

name: Spain
cuisine_summary: Spanish cuisine is one of the world's most regionally diverse and historically significant. The Basque Country alone — with pintxos bars lining every street and more Michelin stars per capita than anywhere on earth — could anchor a world food culture on its own. Catalonia gave the world Ferran Adrià and elBulli, the restaurant that launched molecular gastronomy and changed how every serious chef thinks about cooking. Andalusia invented tapas culture; Valencia invented paella cooked over orange wood in wide shallow pans; the meseta gave Spain jamón ibérico — acorn-fed, 36-month-cured pork leg that many consider the finest cured meat on earth. Spanish food is slow lunches, long evenings, and a deep belief that eating well is not a luxury but a daily right.
dish1_desc: Fried potatoes with smoky tomato sauce and garlic aioli. Bar food, perfected.
dish2_desc: Dry-cured ham from acorn-fed pigs, sliced thin enough to melt on your tongue.
dish3_desc: Saffron rice cooked over fire with seafood or chicken. The crusty bottom (socarrat) is the prize.

name: Sri Lanka
cuisine_summary: Sri Lankan food is coconut-rich and ferociously spiced — the curries here are among the hottest on earth, string hoppers are the breakfast ritual, and kottu roti (chopped flatbread stir-fried on a hot griddle) fills the night air with the clang of metal.
dish1_desc: Ocean or freshwater fish in a fiery coconut milk curry with goraka (dried kokum) for sourness. Deep red, deeply spiced — Sri Lanka's signature curry.
dish2_desc: Delicate rice noodle discs steamed and stacked, eaten for breakfast with coconut sambol and dhal curry. The Sri Lankan morning ritual — light, intricate, quietly perfect.
dish3_desc: Day-old roti chopped on a hot griddle with egg, vegetables, and meat — the rhythm of the metal blades is the sound of Sri Lankan nights. Spicy, textured, and impossible to resist.

name: Sudan
cuisine_summary: Sudanese food is Nile Valley cooking — ful medames is the national breakfast, kissra (fermented sorghum flatbread) is the staple that replaces all other bread, and slow-cooked stews make use of everything the river and land provide.
dish1_desc: Slow-cooked fava beans mashed with peanut butter, cumin, lemon, and chili oil. Sudan's foundational breakfast — eaten across the country, every morning.
dish2_desc: Thin, pliable fermented sorghum flatbread — simultaneously the plate and the utensil. Laid flat and covered in stew, torn and used to scoop every last drop.
dish3_desc: Stew of dried okra, meat, and spices eaten over kissra. Sudan's most characteristic everyday dish — earthy, textured, and tied to the country's agricultural traditions.

name: Suriname
cuisine_summary: Surinamese food is South America's most diverse table — Indonesian, Indian, Chinese, African, and Dutch influences all present at once. Pom (the national dish) is eaten at every party; roti is the everyday street food.
dish1_desc: Taro root grated and baked with chicken, citrus juice, and tomato until set and caramelized. Suriname's most celebratory dish — served at every birthday, wedding, and holiday.
dish2_desc: Flaky, oil-layered roti flatbread wrapped around curried chicken and potato. A legacy of Javanese and Indian indentured labor — Suriname's essential everyday street food.
dish3_desc: Rice cooked with vegetables, salted fish, smoked meat, and coconut milk into a savory one-pot. The Surinamese Creole dish — every family has a version.

name: Sweden
cuisine_summary: Swedish food is New Nordic and old smörgåsbord — meatballs with lingonberry jam, gravlax with dill, and a fika (coffee break) culture that makes cinnamon rolls a civic institution. The new Nordic movement here changed how the world thinks about Scandinavian cooking.
dish1_desc: Small pork-and-beef meatballs pan-fried in butter, served with creamy gravy, lingonberry jam, and pickled cucumber. Sweden's most internationally recognized dish — and genuinely excellent.
dish2_desc: Salmon cured in salt, sugar, and dill for 48 hours, sliced thin and served with hovmästarsås (a sweet mustard-dill sauce). The Swedish way with salmon — delicate and masterful.
dish3_desc: Enriched dough rolled with butter, cinnamon, and cardamom, twisted into a bun. The cinnamon roll of Swedish fika culture — eaten with coffee, never rushed.

name: Switzerland
cuisine_summary: Swiss food is Alpine and trilingual — cheese fondue from the French cantons, rösti potato cake from the German-speaking regions, and risotto from Ticino in the south. The three cuisines are unified by extraordinary dairy and an unhurried pace.
dish1_desc: Gruyère and Emmental melted with white wine, garlic, and kirsch, kept warm over a flame. Bread cubes are dunked on long forks — no double-dipping, and the person who loses a cube buys the wine.
dish2_desc: Coarsely grated potato fried in butter until golden and crispy on both sides. Zürich's great potato dish — eaten as a side or topped with egg and cheese as a meal.
dish3_desc: Raclette cheese melted under a grill and scraped over boiled potatoes, cornichons, and pickled onions. Switzerland's other great cheese ritual — slow, social, and warming.

name: Syria
cuisine_summary: Syrian food is Levantine cooking at its most refined — kibbeh in dozens of forms, the sweetest pomegranate-walnut dips, and a mezze tradition built around hospitality that remains intact despite everything the country has endured.
dish1_desc: Ground lamb and bulgur wheat formed into hollow shells, stuffed with spiced minced meat and pine nuts, then fried or baked. Syria's great dish — endlessly varied by region and occasion.
dish2_desc: Roasted red pepper and walnut paste blended with pomegranate molasses and cumin. Syria's most distinctive mezze dip — smoky, slightly sweet, and completely addictive.
dish3_desc: Toasted flatbread layered with yogurt, chickpeas, and tahini, topped with pine nuts and paprika butter. A Damascus breakfast — crunchy, creamy, layered, and eaten immediately before it softens.

name: São Tomé and Príncipe
cuisine_summary: São Toméan food is West African island cooking with Portuguese colonial roots — fresh Atlantic seafood, palm oil, and calulu (the national stew) that combines dried fish with okra and greens in one pot.
dish1_desc: Dried and fresh fish stewed together with okra, palm oil, tomato, and leafy greens. The national dish — complex, layered, and a product of both Portuguese and African influences.
dish2_desc: Ripe plantain sliced and fried until caramelized. The everyday accompaniment to fish and meat dishes — sweet, simple, essential.
dish3_desc: Chicken stewed in palm oil with tomatoes, onions, and local spices. A traditional São Toméan dish reflecting the islands' African culinary heritage.

name: Taiwan
cuisine_summary: Taiwanese food is Chinese tradition remixed into something entirely its own — night markets that define how to snack, beef noodle soup that is taken as seriously as fine wine, and bubble tea that was invented here before it was everywhere.
dish1_desc: Thick wheat noodles in a slow-cooked beef and soy broth with braised beef shank, pickled mustard greens, and chili oil. Taiwan's national dish — subject to annual competitions and lifelong loyalties.
dish2_desc: Flaky, layered wheat flatbread with scallions, pan-fried until golden and crispy. The Taiwanese street breakfast — made to order and eaten immediately.
dish3_desc: Sweetened milk tea shaken with ice and loaded with chewy tapioca pearls. Born in Taichung in the 1980s — now a global phenomenon that Taiwan invented.

name: Tajikistan
cuisine_summary: Tajik food is Central Asian Silk Road cooking — plov is the great communal rice dish, samsa are the tandoor-baked pastries of every bazaar, and the cuisine is shaped by Persian, Uzbek, and Afghan neighbors.
dish1_desc: Saffron-yellow rice cooked with lamb, yellow carrots, and chickpeas in a kazan (cast iron pot) over open fire. The Tajik centerpiece — made for celebrations, eaten communally.
dish2_desc: Flaky layered pastry filled with spiced lamb and onion, baked in a tandoor oven until puffy and golden. The Central Asian bazaar staple — aromatic and deeply satisfying.
dish3_desc: Clear lamb and vegetable soup with potato, tomato, and fresh herbs. The everyday Tajik restorative — clean, warming, found at every family table.

name: Tanzania
cuisine_summary: Tanzanian food is two distinct worlds — the mainland's ugali-and-stew tradition, and Zanzibar's spice island cooking where Indian Ocean trade routes left cardamom, cloves, and saffron in everything.
dish1_desc: Stiff white maize porridge paired with goat or beef grilled over charcoal. The Tanzanian mainland combination — eaten by hand, communal, completely satisfying.
dish2_desc: Spiced rice cooked with meat and a complex blend of whole spices — cardamom, cloves, cinnamon, cumin. Zanzibar's Indian Ocean-influenced signature dish.
dish3_desc: A tangy, complex street food soup of potato, mango, coconut, cassava, and deep-fried snacks in a tart, curry-spiced broth. Zanzibar's most unique dish — chaotic, sour, unforgettable.

name: Thailand
cuisine_summary: Thai cuisine is one of the world's most harmonically complex — every dish balances sweet, sour, salty, spicy, and umami simultaneously, not sequentially. The cuisine is deeply regional: the north has khao soi (coconut curry noodles) and mild, herb-forward stews; the northeast (Isan) has larb (meat salad with toasted rice powder) and papaya salad with fierce heat; the south has the most ferocious curries, blackened by roasted coconut and dried chiles. Pad thai, massaman curry, and tom yum goong are known globally — but the depth of Thai street food culture, from grilled satay to mango sticky rice, is what earns it a place among the world's great culinary traditions. The mortar and pestle is the soul of the kitchen.
dish1_desc: Wide rice noodles stir-fried with Chinese broccoli, egg, and dark soy. Less sweet than pad thai, more wok smoke.
dish2_desc: Coconut soup with chicken, galangal, lemongrass, and chile. Comforting and bright at the same time.
dish3_desc: Coconut milk curry of fresh green chiles, basil, and chicken or eggplant. Eat over jasmine rice.

name: Timor-Leste
cuisine_summary: Timorese food is Southeast Asian with Portuguese colonial traces — rice and corn are the staples, fresh fish is grilled simply, and the cuisine reflects a country that has long relied on its land and surrounding sea for survival.
dish1_desc: Fresh fish marinated in lime juice, garlic, and chili then grilled over coals. The Timorese coastal everyday dish — simple, fresh, and tied to the sea.
dish2_desc: Corn kernels and mung beans stewed with spinach and coconut milk. The traditional Timorese subsistence dish — nutritious, earthy, and ancient.
dish3_desc: Grilled chicken in a marinade of green herbs, ginger, and spices. Portuguese-influenced and adapted to Timorese flavors — the festive poultry dish.

name: Togo
cuisine_summary: Togolese food is West African staple cooking — fufu pounded tableside is the great communal experience, peanut sauces and palm oil stews are the flavoring agents, and the cuisine sits between Ghanaian and Beninese traditions.
dish1_desc: Pounded yam or cassava fufu eaten by hand with a thick peanut and tomato sauce over meat or fish. The Togolese staple combination — eaten at every main meal.
dish2_desc: Spinach stewed with tomato, onion, and smoked fish in palm oil. One of the most common everyday Togolese dishes — simple, nutritious, full of flavor.
dish3_desc: Steamed fermented corn cakes — slightly spongy, mild, and used to scoop up sauces. A Togolese street food and breakfast staple.

name: Trinidad and Tobago
cuisine_summary: Trinidadian food is the Caribbean's most diverse table — Indian, African, Chinese, Spanish, and French all showing up in one meal. Doubles are the national street food, roti is the daily bread, and the pepper sauce is not optional.
dish1_desc: Two bara (soft fried flatbreads) filled with curried chickpeas (channa), tamarind sauce, and pepper sauce. Trinidad's great breakfast street food — eaten before dawn at roadside stands.
dish2_desc: Dhalpuri (split pea flatbread) or paratha wrapped around curried chicken, goat, duck, or shrimp. The everyday Trinidadian meal — shaped by generations of Indian indenture.
dish3_desc: Rice, pigeon peas, and caramelized chicken cooked together in coconut milk until the bottom chars. The one-pot Trinidadian celebration dish — made for parties, beach lime, and cricket matches.

name: Tunisia
cuisine_summary: Tunisian food is North Africa's most aggressively spiced — harissa (the red chile paste that defines the cuisine) goes into everything. Couscous is the Friday staple, brik is the street snack, and the food is bolder than its Moroccan cousin.
dish1_desc: Thin malsouka pastry folded around a whole egg, tuna, and harissa, then fried until the egg is just set inside. Tunisia's great street snack — eat fast before the yolk runs.
dish2_desc: Steamed semolina with lamb or fish, vegetables, and a fiery broth built on harissa. Tunisia's version is spicier and more pungent than Moroccan couscous — no apologies.
dish3_desc: Chickpea soup poured over stale bread with harissa, cumin, a poached egg, and olive oil. Tunisia's definitive breakfast — earthy, spiced, and energizing.

name: Turkey
cuisine_summary: Turkish cuisine is the heir to Ottoman court cooking — one of the most sophisticated culinary traditions in history, feeding an empire that stretched across three continents. The mezze table arrives first: hummus, baba ganoush, stuffed grape leaves, cheese-filled pastries, and cold vegetable dishes in olive oil. Then the grill: köfte, shish kebab, and the döner that traveled the world and became a global street food. Börek (layered filo with cheese or meat), lahmacun (flatbread with spiced lamb), and pide are the everyday staples. Baklava, Turkish delight, and künefe represent a pastry tradition that spread from Istanbul across the entire former empire. Turkish tea — steeped dark and served in tulip glasses — accompanies all of it.
dish1_desc: Thinly sliced lamb döner laid over torn flatbread, drenched in tomato sauce and browned butter, served alongside yogurt. Bursa's masterpiece — one of Turkey's greatest dishes.
dish2_desc: Scrambled eggs with tomato, green pepper, and spices, cooked in one pan and eaten from it. Turkey's classic breakfast — made in minutes, impossible to improve.
dish3_desc: Layers of paper-thin phyllo filled with pistachios or walnuts and soaked in sugar syrup. Turkey's great pastry — Gaziantep's version uses local pistachios and sets the global standard.

name: Turkmenistan
cuisine_summary: Turkmen food is Central Asian nomadic cooking — lamb plov is the great communal dish, shorba is the everyday soup, and a cuisine shaped by the Karakum Desert and the ancient Silk Road cities of Merv and Nisa.
dish1_desc: Rice cooked with lamb, onion, and carrots in a massive kazan pot over open fire. The Turkmen national dish — made outdoors for gatherings, eaten communally.
dish2_desc: Clear lamb and vegetable broth with chickpeas and potato. The everyday Turkmen restorative — simple, warming, and present at every table.
dish3_desc: Thin circles of dough fried quickly in oil until puffy and golden. The traditional Turkmen flatbread — made fresh and eaten immediately, with tea or alongside stew.

name: Uganda
cuisine_summary: Ugandan food is matoke and groundnuts — steamed green plantain (matoke) is the national staple, groundnut stew is the national sauce, and the Rolex (egg rolled in chapati) is the street food invention the country is quietly very proud of.
dish1_desc: Green plantains steamed inside banana leaves until soft and mashed. Uganda's national dish — the staple of the Ganda people, eaten at every meal in the south.
dish2_desc: A chapati flatbread rolled around fried eggs and vegetables, made fresh at roadside stalls. Uganda's beloved street food — the name is 'rolled eggs,' compressed by habit into something catchier.
dish3_desc: Rich, thick peanut stew with chicken, tomatoes, and onion. The most common sauce eaten with matoke, rice, or posho — deeply satisfying and filling.

name: Ukraine
cuisine_summary: Ukrainian food is Eastern Europe's heartiest — borscht (which Ukraine insists it invented before Russia), varenyky dumplings at every celebration, and salo (cured pork fat on dark bread) that is as deeply embedded in Ukrainian identity as any symbol.
dish1_desc: Vivid red beet and beef soup with cabbage, carrot, and potato, served with sour cream and pampushky (garlic bread rolls). Ukraine claims this — loudly and with historical justification.
dish2_desc: Boiled dumplings filled with potato and cheese, sauerkraut and mushroom, or sweet cherry. Ukraine's great comfort food — served with fried onion and sour cream, eaten at every holiday.
dish3_desc: Cured pork back fat, sliced paper-thin and eaten on dark bread with garlic and raw onion. Ukraine's most traditional and proudly defended food — ancient, simple, and deeply Ukrainian.

name: United Arab Emirates
cuisine_summary: Emirati food is Gulf cooking at its most generous and spice-fragrant — slow-cooked rice with meat and dried lime, date-sweetened desserts, and a hospitality culture where coffee and dates are the first thing you receive in any home.
dish1_desc: Slow-cooked wheat and lamb beaten to a smooth, silky paste and seasoned with a touch of ghee and cinnamon. The UAE's ancient dish — eaten at Ramadan, Eid, and weddings.
dish2_desc: Fragrant spiced rice cooked with meat or fish, dried limes, and rose water. The Emirati national dish — eaten from a communal platter, always with the right hand.
dish3_desc: Deep-fried dough balls drizzled with date syrup and sesame seeds. The UAE's beloved street dessert — crispy outside, soft within, sold at markets and festivals.

name: United Kingdom
cuisine_summary: British food has quietly shed its bad reputation — fish and chips from a good chippie, a Sunday roast with all the trimmings, and a curry culture so thoroughly adopted that chicken tikka masala was once declared the national dish. The full breakfast remains non-negotiable.
dish1_desc: Beer-battered cod or haddock, deep-fried, with thick-cut chips. Eaten from paper with malt vinegar — best at a seaside chippie, debated everywhere else.
dish2_desc: Roast beef (or lamb, chicken, or pork) with Yorkshire pudding, roast potatoes, seasonal vegetables, and gravy. Britain's most sacred weekly ritual — attended rain or shine.
dish3_desc: Yogurt-marinated chicken in a creamy, spiced tomato sauce. Invented in Glasgow or Birmingham by South Asian immigrants — now as British as anything, and genuinely delicious.

name: United States
cuisine_summary: San Francisco and the Bay Area didn't just participate in American food culture — they rewrote it. When Alice Waters opened Chez Panisse in Berkeley in 1971, she launched the California cuisine movement: cook only what's local, seasonal, and sustainably grown. That radical idea gave birth to the farm-to-table movement, the organic food revival, and the farmers' market renaissance now standard across the country. In SF itself, Zuni Café (1979) and Greens (1979) carried that torch. California cuisine also absorbed the city's multicultural reality — Chinese, Japanese, Mexican, and Vietnamese influences folded into a distinctly Californian synthesis. The result elevated American food to a global level, and it started right here.
dish1_desc: Beef brisket rubbed in salt and pepper and smoked over post oak for 12-18 hours until the bark is black and the interior melts. Central Texas's great contribution — patience as technique.
dish2_desc: Creamy New England soup of clams, potato, and salt pork. Boston's signature — best served in a sourdough bread bowl in San Francisco, which is not Boston but somehow makes it work.
dish3_desc: Buttermilk-marinated chicken fried in a heavily seasoned flour crust until shattering-crisp. The American South's most important dish — adopted everywhere, never quite replicated.

name: Uruguay
cuisine_summary: Uruguayan food is Southern Cone beef culture with its own confident identity — the chivito (the national sandwich) is the richest steak sandwich in the world, the asado is slow and wood-fired, and dulce de leche goes on everything.
dish1_desc: A steak sandwich stacked with ham, bacon, fried egg, cheese, olives, and salad in a soft roll. Uruguay's national dish — a full meal held in two hands.
dish2_desc: Wood-fire grilled beef, lamb, and pork over a low parrilla. Uruguay argues it does this better than Argentina. Both are right enough that the argument is worth having.
dish3_desc: Thick, golden milk caramel spread on toast, rolled into pastries, and layered into cakes. Uruguay claims to have invented it — the rest of South America disagrees politely while eating it.

name: Uzbekistan
cuisine_summary: Uzbek food is Central Asia's most celebrated — the plov of Tashkent's masters is a pilgrimage-worthy dish, samsa from a tandoor oven is the bazaar's essential snack, and the Silk Road has left layers of Persian, Chinese, and Russian influence in every dish.
dish1_desc: The Central Asian apex: rice cooked with lamb, yellow carrots, chickpeas, and quail eggs in a kazan over open fire. Uzbekistan's national dish — Tashkent's plov-masters train for years and serve thousands daily.
dish2_desc: Layered pastry filled with spiced lamb and onion, baked against the wall of a tandoor until blistered and fragrant. The Uzbek bazaar staple — flaky, juicy, and eaten standing.
dish3_desc: Hand-pulled noodles in a rich lamb and vegetable broth with tomato and spices. The Silk Road noodle dish — Chinese in ancestry, entirely Uzbek in character.

name: Vanuatu
cuisine_summary: Vanuatu food is Pacific island cooking at its most elemental — laplap (the national dish) is cooked in earth ovens, root vegetables are the staple, and the 83 islands each have their own variations on the same coconut-and-starch theme.
dish1_desc: Grated taro, yam, or banana mixed with coconut milk, wrapped in banana leaves, and cooked in an underground earth oven. Vanuatu's national dish — communal, elemental, and deeply satisfying.
dish2_desc: Laplap with a filling of meat or fish at its center — the stuffed, celebratory version of the national dish. Made for special occasions.
dish3_desc: Giant prawns from Vanuatu's island rivers, grilled or steamed simply. The prized local ingredient — sweet, fresh, and best cooked minutes after being caught.

name: Venezuela
cuisine_summary: Venezuelan food is arepa culture and pabellón criollo — the arepa (corn cake) is eaten at every meal in every form, the national dish layers shredded beef, black beans, rice, and plantain on one plate, and hallacas at Christmas are the most labor-intensive food tradition in the Americas.
dish1_desc: Shredded slow-braised beef, black beans, white rice, and fried sweet plantain on one plate. Venezuela's national dish — the four elements of the country's cooking in one harmonious arrangement.
dish2_desc: Grilled or fried corn cake split open and filled with cheese, beef, chicken, avocado, or all of the above. Venezuela's daily bread — eaten at every meal, by everyone, every day.
dish3_desc: Corn dough filled with a slow-cooked stew of beef, pork, olives, raisins, and capers, wrapped in banana leaves and steamed. Venezuela's Christmas dish — made over three days by the whole family.

name: Vietnam
cuisine_summary: Vietnamese food arrived in San Francisco through one of the most dramatic chapters in the city's history. After the fall of Saigon in 1975, thousands of Vietnamese refugees settled in the Tenderloin — a neighborhood no one else wanted — and transformed Larkin Street into Little Saigon, officially designated in 2003. The two-block stretch is more than 80% Vietnamese-owned. Pho, bánh mì, and bún bò Huế became SF staples. Saigon Sandwich on Larkin has been making bánh mì for 40+ years. It is one of the great immigrant comeback stories in American food history.
dish1_desc: Beef noodle soup in long-simmered broth with star anise and clove. Add basil, sprouts, lime, chile to taste.
dish2_desc: Crusty baguette with pâté, pickled daikon and carrot, cucumber, cilantro, and meat. The Franco-Vietnamese sandwich.
dish3_desc: Spicy lemongrass beef noodle soup from central Vietnam — bolder and more pungent than phở.

name: Yemen
cuisine_summary: Yemeni cuisine is one of the Arabian Peninsula's oldest and most distinctive — shaped by ancient spice trade routes, mountain geography, and coastal fishing traditions. Saltah is the national dish: a meat stew finished with hulba (fenugreek froth) and served bubbling in a stone bowl. Mandi — whole lamb or chicken slow-roasted over smoldering wood in a sealed pit — is the great ceremonial dish, eaten with fragrant rice. Bint al-sahn (honey-drenched flaky bread) is the beloved dessert. Lahoh (a spongy sourdough flatbread) is the breakfast staple. Yemeni food is aromatic without being fiery — spices like hawaij (a warm blend of cumin, turmeric, coriander, and black pepper) perfume the cooking with subtlety and depth.
dish1_desc: Spiced rice with slow-roasted lamb or chicken cooked in a tandoor-like pit. Served on a communal platter.
dish2_desc: Brown meat stew topped with fenugreek froth, eaten with flatbread. Yemen's national dish.
dish3_desc: Flaky honey bread, layered with butter, drizzled with honey, dusted with black seed. Breakfast or anytime.

name: Zambia
cuisine_summary: Zambian food is nshima and relish — stiff white maize porridge is the daily staple eaten at every meal, and the relish (ifisashi, kapenta, or stewed meat) is the supporting cast. The great lakes provide kapenta fish; the land provides everything else.
dish1_desc: Stiff white maize porridge rolled into balls and eaten by hand. The Zambian daily staple — present at breakfast, lunch, and dinner for most of the population.
dish2_desc: Leafy greens cooked in a peanut paste sauce. The most common vegetable relish in Zambia — eaten alongside nshima at every meal.
dish3_desc: Tiny dried lake fish (similar to whitebait) fried or stewed with tomato, onion, and chili. The everyday Zambian protein — fished from the great lakes and eaten across the country.

name: Zimbabwe
cuisine_summary: Zimbabwean food is sadza and the relish beside it — stiff white maize porridge is the national staple, slow-cooked meats and vegetable stews are the sauces, and the cuisine reflects both Shona and Ndebele traditions.
dish1_desc: Dense white maize porridge cooked to a firm consistency and eaten by hand. Zimbabwe's national staple — eaten at every meal, used to scoop up stew, relish, or greens.
dish2_desc: Beef or goat stew with leafy greens (rape or covo), slow-cooked with tomato and onion. The most common accompaniment to sadza — simple, nourishing, everywhere.
dish3_desc: Small dried and salted fish, reconstituted and cooked with tomato and onion into a pungent, savory relish. An affordable everyday protein — pungent, deeply flavorful, and beloved.
